The house resumed from Thursday, April 28, consideration in committee of Bill No. 105, to assist in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress-Mr. Rogers- Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour):	Mr. Chairman, before the committee proceeds further with the bill I should like to refer to certain statements made last night by the lion, member for Temiseouata. In the interval I have had an opportunity of investigating the charge made that Mr. Purvis, as chairman of the national employment commission, had obtained certain information which would be of value to him in his private business associations. That investigation has confirmed the opinion I expressed last night, that the information so obtained was used solely for public purposes. Late in 1936 and early in 1937 a form was sent out under the authority of the national employment commission to the larger employers throughout Canada. The form stated its purpose to be to secure data deemed useful in studying employment and unemployment. to be supplementary to the commission's studies along other lines, such as the registration of direct relief recipients. That form was prepared by the members and officers of the commission. At the close of 1937 a report was issued embodying the information secured from the replies received. This report was issued and was tabled as a matter of fact in this house under the title of Report on Phases of Employment Conditions in Canadian Industry.
In no sense was it the thought or intention of the commission to look into the circumstances of individual firms; in fact an undertaking was given on the form itself to the effect that nothing of that nature would be done. This undertaking read as follows:
In so far a's the individual firm is concerned this reply will be treated as absolutely confidential. Information taken from the forms will be made public only in a general way: in no case will publicity be given to the individual return nor will it be available to any other branch of government.
That promise was most scrupulously carried out.
The work of receiving the forms and of collecting the data which they contained was under the direction of V. C. Phelan, director of registration, who was serving as an officer of the commission at the time. Neither the chairman nor any member of the commission ever asked for any one of the individual returns and none was shown to them. In order to discharge the project effectively it was unnecessary for the commission even to see these individual returns, as the purpose had been to secure data by classes, and when the data was ready in that form it was carefully considered by the commissioners.
A copy of the published report was sent to each employer who had submitted a return and no one has forwarded an objection to the use made of the information which he supplied. On the other hand, the commission was in receipt of statements from some employers to the effect that they considered the facts brought to light to be of value and that they appreciated receiving the report.
To sum up: the fact is that no one has at any time had possession of or been privileged to read the individual returns except the staff engaged in the statistical compilation, and steps were taken to see that the undertaking made to reporting firms was scrupulously regarded. It is a matter of opinion whether the individual employer's return in this case would be of assistance to a business competitor, as the information sought did not deal with the financial set-up or the producing, sales or commercial policies of firms.
I should just like to say in conclusion, repeating what I said last night, that Mr. Purvis as chairman, and Mr. Tom Moore as vice chairman, and all the members of the commission, approached their task as public-spirited citizens with a keen sense of responsibility, and I regret exceedingly that the hon. member has seen fit to make accusations against public servants who have been faithful and conscientious in the performance of their duties.

Mr. Chairman, last July the national employment commission devoted a bulletin to an article on the "unscrambling of this business of relief." In this hulletin it is suggested that we ought to have a division between unemployment relief and agricultural assistance, and in the case of the unemployed we ought to distinguish very clearly between those who are unemployed and those who are unemployable. I wonder if the minister can give any reason why various types of assistance should continue to be lumped in this way.
The other question I would ask is whether the minister could tell us the principles which are to guide the dominion government in the giving of relief during this coming season. I should like to know a little more clearly just what program is contemplated by the government, how extensive it will be, and along what particular lines.

speechtext:
First, as to the division of relief recipients into a number of classes towards which various governmental bodies should have a special responsibility, that is a question that has engaged the attention not only of this administration and of provincial governments but also of previous administrations who have had to deal with the question from the standpoint both of the dominion government and of the provinces. When direct relief was instituted in this country it was done, perhaps necessarily, without any classification of relief recipients upon the basis of their employability. It is possible-I do not wish to be dogmatic about it-that if the employment service of Canada had been used as the mechanism for dealing with relief from the beginning you might have had that division between unemployables and employables. But that was not found practicable. The result is that you have had on relief lists in practically all municipalities a mixture of unemployables and employables, including many cases which were formerly dealt with

Relief and Agricultural Distress
by private charity. That being the situation, we are confronted with the desirability of resolving that general problem into its constituent elements. It has not been easy, and the problem is complicated by the fact that these relief lists have been developing along the basis I have indicated within the past few years.
As I have mentioned to the committee before, in the agreements which were in operation during the last quarter of the past fiscal year we have sought to get the provinces to cooperate with us in a definition of unemployability. That again is a question which requires experience, in order to determine what your standard of unemployability shall be. We are proceeding largely upon the basis of physical and mental infirmities in determining unemployability, but we have not up to this time by our own action placed the responsibility for unemployables wholly upon the municipalities. Some provinces have done that of their own volition. As a matter of fact some provinces followed more or less that line of division from the beginning, but that was the exception rather than the rule.
My hon. friend has asked what will be done during the present year in that regard. I can tell him that we propose, with the cooperation of the provinces, to secure a more efficient division of the groups of relief recipients.

I mean that the definition of unemployability which was in effect during the last quarter of the past fiscal year may have to be revised to some extent. In the light of experience in the last few months with the provinces, we hope to bring about a much more effective division of relief recipients, but not at the same time attempting to place the responsibility for unemployables upon any particular governmental agency. As I have mentioned, the provinces Ihemselves in some cases placed the care of unemployables back upon the municipalities or upon private charities.
Now as to the measures which should be taken by the government for the provision of relief during the forthcoming year, that of course will be dealt with by items in the supplementary estimates as in the past two years, and in the allocation of the grant in aid to the provinces we shall be governed by the actual unemployment conditions in the various provinces, and also shall see to it that the division is one which will enable the dominion government to gain, if there is an improvement in the employment situation, in common with both the provinces and the municipalities who are equally concerned.

I can tell him, however, that these plans will be continued and extended.
As to other provisions for relief-land settlement, for instance-there are agreements with several provinces and provision will be made therefor. Relief settlement agreements apply only in a number of provinces. But again, the committee is aware that our experience in connection with the settlement of families on relief in rural areas has not been of uniform success. Provision will be made also to deal with the drought situation

in the western provinces, because the present provision has extended only up to the fiscal year. I would say, however, in that connection, that in July of last year, in order to bring about a more effective administration of relief in the drought areas, all relief in those areas was brought under the Department of Agriculture. In other words, that department now deals with both relief for human beings and relief in other forms in the drought area.

Yes, that was a departure from the former policy. With respect to most of these expenditures on relief, we have had to work in cooperation with the provinces. That, again, is not something new; it has existed from the beginning. In other words, through grants in aid and financial assistance we deal with those who are in direct contact with the administration of relief.
I understand the desire of my hon. friend for more ample information at this time. There are two courses of action that might be followed. We could bring in supplementary estimates first and then deal with the relief bill, but that would be illogical, because we cannot make expenditures under the supplementary estimates until we have the relief legislation. It is under this authority that money is expended for the relief of unemployment and agricultural distress, and therefore we proceed first with this bill, in order to obtain the necessary authority to make expenditures either directly or in cooperation with the provinces, and then bring in supplementary estimates, for which, of course, the government will be fully responsible when they are submitted. They will be fully exposed to the criticism of my hon. friend or of any others in the house on the basis of the policies therein outlined.

Is the minister aware that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Vancouver East have just stated an opinion that is held very widely in the country and in this house? I know that a resolution was brought down foreshadowing this bill. We have had the bill before us, and yet we have no information regarding the government's intentions. It seems to me that with this pressing problem, as with other pressing problems, it is in the interests of the government and of the minister himself that the house should be taken into the full confidence of the administration. It strikes me, as it does many others in this house, that there is too much secrecy with regard to the intentions of the government and the legislation to be placed before parliament, and I would therefore impress upon the minister the fact that the opinions that have been expressed this afternoon are opinions that are very widely held throughout the country and among members on both sides of this house.
When the minister rose first to speak in this chamber two years ago we all looked to him to give a real lead in the solution of the unemployment problem; but in two years very little of a constructive nature has been accomplished, and when we examine the report of the national employment commission it is with a great deal of misgiving that we see recommendation after recommendation either not considered, or no action or only partial action taken. Throughout this country, as those who have been across it within the last few weeks must be aware, there is a rising tide of discontent with the inactivity of this parliament. As one who believes in democracy

and the maintenance of our democratic institutions I say that the present government of Canada is doing more to undermine our democratic institutions than all the subversive propaganda that can be spread across the country. Everywhere one hears criticism of the inactivity of the present parliament. I rise to the defence of the minister in that respect. In answer to what the three hon. gentlemen have just said, let me state that the government must be empowered by parliament to act with regard to unemployment. This is why the bill is now before the committee. In order to do something the government must first be given the power to do it. There is a very good reason for this procedure; it is that when the bill is discussed in committee every member of the committee can make any suggestion, and I am sure that the minister has taken careful note of the suggestions which have just been made by the three hon. members *who have spoken. It is after having full knowledge of the needs of their own constituencies and those of hon. members who sit here now that the government can meet in council and see what according to their judgment it is best to do under the circumstances. If this bill were passed as expeditiously as the divorce bills, probably there would be before the committee an item in the supplementary estimates dealing with the matters just referred to by the hon. gentlemen. The sooner the bill is dealt with the sooner the government will be in a position to submit concrete figures and give the information asked for by the hon. gentlemen. On the other hand, since I Lave been a member of this house I have repeatedly been told that the meetings of the privy council are secret, and that the ministers are pledged not to divulge anything that goes on in the council. It would be most improper for the minister to mention any discussion that has taken place in council before the quorum of council decides to give it to the house and the country. I am sure that these explanations will be satisfactory to the hon. gentlemen.

May I make a suggestion to the minister? Until now every government in this country, every legislative body, whether federal or provincial, has paid attention only to the unemployed on relief. There is another class of unemployed deserving of equal consideration; it is the class of unemployed not on relief. Let me illustrate. As to the case of a family of five-father, mother, and three children on relief-I need not give any further explanation. But take the case of a father ind mother not on relief who have to look ifter their children and support them just the same. Suppose there are boys or girls capable of working, say one girl and two boys of ages from eighteen to twenty-four. They have no work, and the family is looking after them. This kills their initiative. These young men deserve consideration. This morning in the civil service committee Sir Francis Floud, British high commissioner, gave most interesting information about the entry of youth into the British civil service.

First I thank the hon.
member for Temiscouata for directing attention to the proper relationship between this bill and the supplementary estimates which will follow. On that point I would simply say that had there not been established the practice of having annual bills, no question of the kind just raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would have arisen. In other words, the policy of the government in relation to unemployment would have been set out in supplementary estimates and debated when those estimates were before the house. But for some years we have proceeded by way of annual legislation. I am quite free to confess that sometimes I have been in doubt as to whether that was a wise policy; as to whether it might not be preferable simply to put through legislation which would extend without limit of time. However, we are proceeding in this way. This method does not differ in any respect from the way in which we have dealt with this question in previous years, and clearly the government will be responsible for the estimates submitted to this parliament to deal with unemployment and relief, and at that time there will be the fullest opportunity for any hon. member to take exception to what we are doing, to criticize us either because we have gone too far or because we have not gone far enough.
A moment ago one hon. member referred to the fact that he had expected that this government would have been able to accomplish more in the way of solving unemployment than had been the case during the past two or three years. I need hardly say that the wish to make progress in the solution of this problem is felt on this side of the house as strongly as in any other part of the house. As a matter of fact when we see the actual reduction of what .might be termed the controllable unemployment in this country I think we have good reason for satisfaction. The other day I received from the League of Nations economic section a statement dealing with unemployment in all countries reporting to the league, and the position of Canada is one that at least gives us cause for satisfaction in a comparative way. I am quite sure that other hon. members of this house have had an opportunity of seeing at close range the results that have accrued in other countries with respect to unemployment policies. It is a problem that has been with us steadily since the war years. I imagine it would be fair to say that almost every proposal that has been put
forward in this country has been adopted by the administration in the United States, yet the situation with regard to unemployment in that country at present is worse rather than better than it is in this country. I do not say that with any satisfaction; I merely point it out as illustrating the fact that we are dealing with a problem which appears to be inherent in the economic structure which has grown up following the great war.
At this time I am not going to attempt to deal with the immediate and remote causes of economic insecurity. That problem is with us. As I have said on other occasions, it is undoubtedly the great problem of our generation; but I am bound to say that in my most optimistic moments, when I came to the Department of Labour, I did not feel that we were going to be able to liquidate this problem completely in two or three years. I felt that by following wise policies and by assisting natural economic laws we would make definite progress, and I think we have made definite progress. I think we have some cause for satisfaction in that. I agree, however, that we have no ground whatever for that kind of satisfaction which leads to inertia. I fully accept the suggestion that this government must face this problem as it exists at the present time and as we believe it is likely to develop in the next twelve months; and I am bound to say that there are certain obscurities in the unemployment situation as it may develop in succeeding months. The government has its responsibility in connection with that problem, and I can say very definitely that we shall meet that responsibility with the light that we have when the supplementary estimates are brought down.
Now I must give a belated answer to the hon. member for Temiscouata, who has asked just what service might be rendered by the statistical compilation contained in the report of the national employment commission. I would say to him that this statistical compilation or classification of the unemployed is only one, the most recent, monthly calculation made by the registration staff of the commission. It does not represent a complete report. The registration is a continuous process, and one of the great advantages has been that the municipalities that report to the registration branch now report upon the basis of an agreed classification of the unemployed. Not all that information, of course, can be presented in press releases from time to time, but the municipalities themselves, and through the municipalities the relief offices and .the employment service, can have the benefit of a more accurate classification of the unemployed on relief than

Relief and Agricultural Distress
existed before the registration was commenced. The results obtained under the registration are by no means perfect as yet. There are certain delays incident to the dependence of the registration branch upon the municipalities for these returns, which are longer than one could wish, but we are dealing with the registration upon the basis of its performing a very useful service, and certainly we have understood from the municipalities concerned that they appreciate the service rendered in this respect.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I thank the minister for what he has just said, but on the other hand it is impossible to use in any practical way the report of the national employment commission. What they have accomplished during nearly two years, at a cost of over $400,000, is worth absolutely nothing, and I should like the minister to admit it. It would be much better for him to admit that the report is no good, throw it in the waste-paper basket and start anew. That is my humble contention. Why keep it as an heirloom, this blue book which is of no use? There are waste-paper baskets in evety room in this building; there must be some in this chamber. If not I will throw it on the floor. It is no good. Moreover I say that those who signed this report, instead of being praised for having performed a splendid public service, should be severely censured by this house because they did a bad job; just the same as a bootblack who does not shine your boots well; just the same as a gardener who ruins your rose bush; just the same as a cook who burns your meat; just as any other employee is censured. They were working for us.
There is one thing I have wanted to say for a very long time. It is that in this country we have a false idea about men in the public service. Mark you, sir; it has come about that a man is judged by the position he occupies, though very often it is the position that makes the man and not the man that [DOT]makes the position. It makes all the difference in the world. Also if a man is very well off, if he is a millionaire, he is considered a supplementary edition of the Encyclopedia Britan-nica. We have a false idea about these things. A man may be a millionaire and a very able man in his own domain; a man may be a millionaire and not be an able man at all. He may be a millionaire by luck, just as a prospector may find a gold mine and sell it for two million dollars; he is a lucky man, and there are such. There are men who become millionaires because of their own brains. That is all right; they have certain experience in regard to certain things. It is

true that the chairman of that commission employs a large number of men; I admit that, but among the men on his payrolls we do not find one single unemployed. This is something that certain hon. members seem to have forgotten. The report which is now on the floor deals with the unemployed, not with the employed. This man who is a great employer knows nothing about the unemployed. He does not know as much about the unemployed as any hon. member who receives them in his office or visits them in their homes.
Because a man is a leader in industry, it does not follow that he is a leader in every domain. Some think that because a man is rich he must therefore be a deep well of knowledge about everything. I do not say that such a man has not considerable knowledge, but the fact remains that those who consider that a man is a deep well of knowledge simply because he is a millionaire are worshipping the golden calf as they did in olden times. They are worshipping a bankroll. I am not against millionaires, but Mr. Purvis did not do a good job because he is a millionaire. That job was a rotten job. I have said that already and I shall repeat it just as long as I refer to this matter.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) said last night that Mr. Tom Moore was not here to defend himself. Of course he was not here. His place is not in this house and he cannot be here unless we call him before the bar to give an explanation about the way he has acted. We discuss certain things among ourselves just as Mr. Purvis and his directors discuss certain things in the board room. This House of Commons is our board room. I am always surprised when we are told not to say anything about a public servant who cannot be here to defend himself. No one is attacking these people; we are simply judging them. If I say anything unpleasant about one of my colleagues, I may be considered to be attacking him because we are both on the same footing. But on the other hand I have the right to judge a man in the public service, either favourably or unfavourably, according to the dictates of my conscience. I have not attacked anyone; I have been judging. I have judged this man severely because he has been wrongly boosted. I ask the minister to do the same thing as I did-to throw this report on the floor where the sweeper can come along and put it with the other garbage.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Might I ask the minister the present situation with regard to the single unemployed? A serious situation is developing on the Pacific coast in connection with em-

Relief and Agricultural Distress
ployable young men. who are drifting into the cities, particularly Vancouver. I understand that the forestry projects have been or are being closed up and that as a result a total of about 5,000 men will be released. There are also many young transients drifting in from the prairies. Apparently the province will do nothing about caring for these men from the camps and the city must either feed them or face the possibility of riots. In other years there has been trouble of this kind; for example these men have gone out with tin cans and put on unofficial tag days, with the result that hundreds have been put in gaol in the last two years, although they are not criminals in any sense of the word. Many of the men are returned men. The city must either take care of them or adopt these drastic measures.
I do not know the situation with regard to the young men who have been placed on farms. Perhaps they have a chance of obtaining work during the summer on the farms on which they were placed during the winter, but the men from the forestry camps cannot be taken into the forest industries of our province in any large numbers. The minister has stated that the government intends to initiate works which will take care of many of these men. I suggest that the government should assume responsibility for the men coming out of the forestry camps and other transients until such time as they can be placed on these government works, as was done two years ago when men were placed on railway maintenance work. I cannot over-emphasize the seriousness of the situation. We are likely to have riots in Vancouver within the next few days, because the city simply cannot provide for these men. I urge upon the government the necessity of prompt action, and I should like the minister to tell us now what the government proposes to do about it.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The problem of transients
and single homeless men has been dealt with in two ways in the past few years. In the prairie provinces we have provided for them by means of the farm employment plan. That plan has usually gone into operation in October and continued until the first of May, the termination being set by the normal resumption of seeding operations throughout the western provinces. During the past year we have had placements of up to 45,000, in round figures, in the three western provinces. The report suggests, and our experience confirms it, that because of the placing of these single homeless men on farms, for the time being at least there has been a relief of the pressure upon the larger cities and towns in the western provinces. As a matter of fact,
an officer of the Department of Labour travelled to western Canada and British Columbia a few weeks ago to review the entire situation.

speechtext:
The fact is that the farm
placement scheme has hardly been used in British Columbia.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I quite agree. It was
realized in the beginning that the farm employment plan would have a very limited application in British Columbia and it was therefore supplemented by the forestry plan carried out in cooperation with the provincial government. That plan has continued normally from either October or November up until the first of May. That has been the situation during the winter months of this year. It is true that advices have been received recently that due to the slackening of woods operations in British Columbia there has been an increase in the number of single unemployed and transients in the city of Vancouver, but we are keeping in close touch with developments. It always has been a problem to decide when these forestry camps could be suitably closed. We are watching the situation very carefully in cooperation with the provincial government. There never has been a time to my knowledge when these special plans have been continued through the summer months. They have been designed to afford employment and shelter to this particular group of unemployed during the severe winter months.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: It does not help very much to watch the problem; something should be done about it. The minister has admitted that the situation this year with regard to work in the forest industries of British Columbia is not as good as formerly. I suggest to him earnestly and with as much force as I can command that these forestry camps should be kept open until these men can be placed at other work, such as the projects which the government has in mind. The situation is serious and the city has its back right up against the wall. The federal government watches the situation, the provincial government watches the situation, but the city has to deal with these men. This means that home-owners in the city have to pay the shot. It is entirely unfair. I think the situation is far more serious in Vancouver than it is in any other city in Canada, and I would ask the minister if these camps cannot be kept open until something is done about giving the men work.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
With regard to the five or six thousand young men concentrated in Vancouver, and who are without employ-



Relief and Agricultural Distress
ment, may we hear from the minister what provision is being made now for these men? Special provision was made by the Vancouver city council for ex-service men included in that group; was that provision supported in any degree toy his department?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: As to the special provision that has been made for single unemployed men in British Columbia, the agreement has been extended through the present month, and under the arrangement made the men in the forestry camps receive deferred pay, so that certainly the majority of those leaving the camps would have some of their deferred pay coming to them in the ensuing weeks. I am not able to say just at the present time how many of those men are in a position where they might be dependent upon the city of Vancouver or any other municipality in British Columbia to which they might go. We do not ourselves control the administration of these camps, as my hon. friend is fully aware. We contribute under an agreement with the province toward the care of the single unemployed men during the winter months. It is a matter for consideration whether it is wise to close the camps now or later. That question, as I have said, has been before us in other years, and in dealing with it we shall naturally be guided by the best opinion we can obtain as to the need for continuing these camps beyond the date now set for their termination.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I do not agree with the minister when he says that the war is responsible for unemployment.

People are unemployed simply because they cannot secure work, and I want the minister to give us the reasons why they cannot secure work. The employment commission has said that relief rates are competing with wages. In Calgary at the present time the unemployed are on a relief strike. They are simply asking for a living scale that will provide them with

sufficient food, clothing and shelter to keep them from starving. I should like to know, and I think the committee would also, what the relief scales are in the Dominion of Canada -the highest scale that is paid, and just what is the scale that is paid anywhere in Canada that is competing with wages.

was why I objected a while ago to including all of these classes needing assistance in one bill. That is what I am pleading for right along.
As far as the present situation is concerned we have had from the minister a most unsatisfactory statement as to what is likely to be done in British Columbia. Some of us had to take quite an active part in the house three or four years ago, when there was a trek of the unemployed and the Regina

Relief and Agricultural Distress
trekkers, as they were called, were coming east. Does the statement of the minister not mean in effect that this government is going to wait and wait and watch and wait until there are riots in British Columbia, and then when there is rioting we shall turn out the mounted police and people will be killed? Is the minister
waiting for that? I know the minister is a humane man; I have known him for a good many years.

I hate to say that, but that is the logic of the situation, and it does seem to me that those of us who have been through this kind of thing three or four times already must point out the possibilities to the minister. I urge that he ought to take the matter very seriously and not simply " watch " the situation until some untoward incident happens and then be forced to come to the relief of the citizens.
In my own city things are hardly as bad, but about a week ago, during the Easter recess, I sat in with a special committee of the city council of Winnipeg. They were almost in desperation as to what to do. They were urging a housing scheme. They pointed out that there are 5,700 employable male heads of families on relief. Of that number, 850 are building trades artisans and 1,200 building trades labourers. They urged that the best thing that could be done was to launch some sort of slum clearance and housing scheme. What is the government preparing to do? The farm relief plan to which the minister referred, when dealing with matters in Vancouver city is not going to help either the single unemployed or these artisans in Winnipeg and their families. All the goodwill which the minister may express in this chamber is not going to help. We must have some plan worked out by which these men can be given work. That has to be done, and that, this government is not doing.
I shall make one more reference to a frequently quoted document, and then I shall have done, for the time being anyway-

speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman just one question: did the ratepayers of the city of Winnipeg vote last fall in the municipal elections against a housing by-law?

speechtext:
I am not prepared to discuss that. I do not for the moment recall
fMr. Woodsworth.]
whether they did. In any case the answer would involve the whole question of the terms of the by-law. I am not going to discuss the provisions of a particular by-law which Winnipeg might or might not be able to finance; what I am emphasizing is the necessity of this government instituting some scheme by which this building labour can be employed.
I was about to refer to a statement made by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the night of the general elections, October 14, 1935. One paragraph of his speech, which deals with this particular question before us, is as follows:
In the new era which dawns to-day, the struggle for the rights of the people will, in the realm of economic liberty and security, be carried on as never before. Poverty and adversity, want and misery, are the enemies which Liberalism will seek to banish from our land. They have lain in wait at the gate of every Canadian home during the past five years, and their menacing mien has served to destroy the souls, as well as the minds and bodies, of an ever increasing number of men, women and children in our land. We take up at once, as our supreme task, the endeavour to end poverty in the midst of plenty, starvation and unnecessary suffering in a land of abundance, discontent and distress in a country more blessed by Providence than any other on the face of the globe, and to gain for individual lives, and for the nation as a whole, that "health and peace and sweet content" which is the rightful heritage of all.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: He did not blame that on the war, did he?

speechtext: What do we find in this measure before us? Something which is much along the line of previous years. Remember that this government has now been in power for three years.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
