subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Well, this is the third session. The statement which I read was given in October, 1935, and we are getting well on into the third session. We have had a special commission dealing with the matter. The commission has reported. The government has had ample opportunity, even since this house has been in session, of drafting its plans. Yet what do we find? I am going to read one paragraph from this bill.
The governor in council may-
Note that. You may say it is a legal phrase, but it is very suggestive.
The governor in council may out of moneys appropriated by parliament authorize the execution of such undertakings as the governor in council may determine to be in the general . interest of Canada and requisite for the pur-

Relief and Agricultural Distress
poses of this act, and for such purposes may authorize the performance of such acts and the execution of such agreements and contracts as the governor in council may deem necessary and expedient.
That is all we have in this third year. The government may do something; the government is to have power to do something. This type of legislation introduced some years ago as emergency legislation is coming to be the regular thing, and in spite of protests throughout the session, in spite of persistent protests, which perhaps the government regards as unwarranted, we cannot get anything except "Oh well, wait until the supplementaries are down." I should like to know what is going to happen then. Last year we were told to wait until we received the report of the employment commission, and the wonder is that we have not been told to-day in connection with grants in aid that we shall have to wait until the Rowell commission reports. In the meantime the people are suffering and many of our municipalities are bankrupt. It is absolutely unreasonable that this house should be asked to accept these very general statements that have been made to-day with regard to what the government proposes to do in this matter, which even the minister himself suggests is about the most important before the country at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that nothing has been done outside this emergency legislation. I think he will be fair enough to admit that within the last two years $30,000,000 in connection with home building and home improvement has been spent in Canada, made possible by virtue of legislation apart altogether from this. My hon. friend says that that is nothing, but competent authorities say that eighty-five per cent of that $30,000,000 went into wages, and that must have contributed something towards easing the problem.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
It is a common practice on this side of the chamber to have a crack at the government, but that does not extend all the way across, and I hope that I shall always belong to that group of people who judge justly and give honour to whom honour is due. The statement has been put on Hansard frequently that this government has done nothing. As I see it, the function of the government is to pass legislation in the interest of the citizens. Before I came here this session I was asked most vigorously to encourage the Minister of Labour to keep on doing what he has been doing for the youth of Canada. No one can say that nothing was done last year for them. Much of the cause of unemployment at the head of the lakes, to whatever extent unemployment exists, was the lack of a crop in Saskatchewan and in the drought area in the western provinces. No one can stand up and say that nothing was done for Saskatchewan this spring, that no legislation was passed for that province in connection with fodder and feed and grain. I do not think that any man can be honest and make the statement that nothing has been done for Saskatchewan and Alberta.
What is the cause of unemployment? When we get that question clearly settled we shall be able to get somewhere. The Minister of Labour reminds me of a little fellow who used to do some boxing; when you thought you had him down he would -bob up again. I am glad to see the minister coming to the top so frequently, and if I may be pardoned a colloquial expression, I would urge him to step on the gas and continue the good work he is doing for the youth of the country. He will find that they are behind him. I would' also urge the government through him, or through some other source, to complete our great highway, and if possible, to do even more than has been done in connection with small houses, because in my opinion there is nothing that will create so much employment as the housing scheme.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
May I offer a suggestion or two to the minister in connection with this bill, so that when the supplementary estimates are brought down he will have my views before him on a certain phase of the work that has been earned on up to the present time.
Last fall I had the pleasure of joining the minister when he visited my riding and inspected the youth camps that were established in the Sandilands forest reserve. Three camps were established there under an agreement with the province. They entailed an expenditure of $100,000. There was accommodation in each of them for ninety young men. When the minister visited the riding we went to these camps together, and the boys there gave him a reception of which I think he ought to be proud. It was a reception that told him that these boys appreciated what he as Minister of Labour and his efficient staff were trying to do in order to solve a part of the youth problem. There were 270 boys in the three camps. They were paid 21 cents an hour and the work they did was really beyond anything I expected myself in the way of clearing fire hazards. That is something that is greatly beneficial to any forest reserve. The work instilled a sense of discipline in the boys and made them feel
Relief and Agricultural Distress

that they had some responsibility and were playing a part in the affairs of Canada. Personally I take a very deep interest in these camps, not because I expect any political advantage, but because I think they are a splendid thing. The boys were well disciplined, they had a keen sense of their responsibility, and in talking with the officials in charge of the camps I discovered that nearly seventy-five per cent of the wages they were receiving after their board had been paid was assigned to their dependents either in Winnipeg or wherever they had come from. After paying their board they had $16 or $17 left for the month and nearly seventy-five per cent of that was sent to their dependents.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: And that was done voluntarily.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Yes, there was no compulsion about it. When the minister brings down his supplementary estimates, after the house has allowed him to pass this bill authorizing him to do so, I hope he will not forget to give these boys full consideration. I hope he will increase the grants in order to continue these camps and so take care of our youth. In my opinion, the plan of forestry camps is one of the best schemes for the youth of Canada undertaken by this government, and I wish to commend the minister. I would ask him not to forget to increase the amount when he brings down his estimates.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
This bill provides that the dominion government may authorize the execution of certain undertakings in the provinces. We should have a more definite statement from the minister with regard to projects that may be undertaken in the provinces. The season is getting late and road work and other development work should start. Surely the provincial governments and the government here at Ottawa have conferred on these matters.
The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) on behalf of the minister invited suggestions. I am therefore going to make a few suggestions regarding projects which if carried out would be of benefit not only to the provinces but to the whole dominion.
I suggest that the government should undertake the establishment or development of several national parks, particularly in Saskatchewan. I shall mention only one or two, although there are many parts of the province where parks could be established. First there is the Moose Mountain district. That district is in the constituency of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), so I know I shall have his support in this anyway. The Moose
[Mr. Beaubien.j
Mountain district is very picturesque, well treed, with many fresh water lakes teeming with fish, and among visitors from the United States it is fast becoming a popular summer resort. Then in the Qu'Appelle valley near or surrounding the Qu'Appelle lakes is an excellent locality for a national park. The winding Qu'Appelle valley is one of the beauty spots of Saskatchewan, and is already a popular summer resort, United States visitors coming even that far north.
In order to get to these parks, when they are established, roads will be necessary. I suggest the construction of hard-surfaced roads north from the United States boundary through the Moose Mountain district, connecting with No. 9 highway and proceeding north to the Qu'Appelle valley, entering the Qu'Appelle valley at the foot of Crooked lakes, and winding right up to Fort Qu'Appelle. It should be hard-surfaced at least as far north as the Qu'Appelle valley. It would cross No. 1 highway near the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway, and tourist traffic could then turn either east or west; it would at least be in the province. Building and hard-surfacing the roads and development of the parks would provide work for thousands of men now unemployed.
I have here a statement of what the tourist trade meant last year to Quebec-$77,000,000 to that one province; so it is easy to see what it must mean to the whole country. I quote from a speech made in Regina on Monday last by Governor Langer of North Dakota, to representatives of boards of trade and the Saskatchewan motor club. It is recorded that Premier Patterson was there and Hon. Mr. Dunn, the minister of highways. The governor of North Dakota condemned the highways in Saskatchewan as disgraceful. That is something for us to consider, that the governor of a state just to the south should come to Regina and declare that the roads in Saskatchewan are a disgrace. He stated that last year tourist traffic had brought $10,000,000 to the state of North Dakota. He said it was only logical and right to suggest that the province of Saskatchewan endeavour to get this tourist traffic to come further north, but he said that when tourists enter Canada at the southern boundary they go a few miles and then turn back discouraged by road conditions. This is something that we should take into consideration. Such a project would mean much not only to Saskatchewan but to other parts of the dominion as well. I know the Minister of Finance regards the tourist trade as very important, and it would be a great help to Saskatchewan to develop tourist traffic there. The government would do well

Relief and Agricultural Distress
to consider this suggestion and assist the provincial government by spending money on projects such as this.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: As a new member of this house I have had very little to say, but I have listened-sometimes with interest, and sometimes otherwise-to a great many speeches since coming here. We on this side have been keeping rather silent regarding this question of unemployment, but we have heard innumerable speeches on it from the opposite side. Anyone who is fortunate or unfortunate enough to be getting copies of Hansard would form the impression that this dominion is teeming with unemployed men and women and with men, women and children who are not properly clothed or housed or fed.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Isn't that a fact?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: If it is I am not aware of it. Certainly it is not in my riding. Where are they? I should like hon. members who are always telling us of these .people in dire distress to tell me just where they are.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Read the report of the welfare board in Ottawa and you will find out.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Well, let us take Ottawa. How is it that young men from the counties around Ottawa can come right in from the farms and pick up jobs here in the summer? Why is it that girls from the counties around Ottawa can come in and get jobs any time they want, at good pay? Go into the country in the Ottawa valley and look for young men who cannot get a job. I do not know where they are. Our farm boys can ge.t jobs anywhere in the country.-

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Well, take my own riding. I was elected in the spring of last year, and any time I visited Pembroke after my election I would meet numbers of men supposed to be unemployed looking for jobs. But I could go out through the farming districts and never hear a word of unemployment. Our boys go out and find their own jobs, and our girls do the same. I met two girls on the -train a couple of weeks ago, and I knew as soon as I saw them that they must have come from Renfrew county; they do not grow girls like that in the cities. They told me they come in here in the fall after working on the farm in the summer and can choose jobs out of seven or eight offered and go to work immediately at $35 a month with board and lodging. I could take you to one restaurant in this city where three sisters
from one of the farms out here in Russell county are working at good pay; at least when they come out of the door you see them dolled up in fine fur coats.
If you want me to I can tell you just why you have so many young people asking for relief in the cities. Here is an example. I mentioned the two girls I met on the train, who were working in the city. One of them had to go home for Christmas. Her mistress was a very fine woman to work for, and she went to a family on relief in the city where there was a girl eighteen or twenty years of age, and offered that girl $1.50 a day to come and stay with her during those two weeks. The girl came. She was no good but the woman wanted her to stay anyway. She would not stay; she went back on relief. These young people from the farms get jobs because they are not only willing to work; they are eager to work. They attack their work with eagerness, and because they have that ambition they can come right in and take jobs from under the noses of people living in cities and towns.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: They must be Liberals.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: They are good people, anyway. I think it is a godsend to men or women to have been brought up on a farm where they learned how to work without depending on the government to support them. That is one of the curses of the situation we are drifting into; we are sending out propaganda all over the country getting people to think that the federal government should take charge of all their worries, instead of educating our people to use their own initiative to make a living.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Where can they get work? .

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: How do our boys get work? They just drift away and get jobs anywhere they want them. I can tell you that as far as North Renfrew is concerned there was not an employable unemployed man getting relief for the last six months of last year.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: That is a small section of Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Perhaps it is, but when will we ever get rid of relief? The suggestion is that the federal government ought to assume the responsibility, and we had the mayors of the cities getting together and insisting that the federal government take over all this burden of relief. When will we ever get rid of it? Take all the responsibility off the municipalities and you will have relief forever. In the township in which I live, and

Relief and Agricultural Distress
in most of the townships in North Renfrew, we never went on relief; we were afraid to start it because we thought we might never get it stopped. There were times when we could have put a third of the township on relief if we had wished; they were just as deserving as a great many other people on relief, but we did not do it, and we pulled through. If we ran across needy cases we looked after them out of our own township funds, rather than have the reputation of going on relief, and I could tell you of villages that did the same thing. I remember one case in particular, where we fought for a year or two to keep a certain family off relief. Finally the man's house was burned down and he flitted away; but before he flitted away he bought a brand new Ford car to go away with. Recently that man went through our municipality with a trailer behind his car and his wife sitting at the table all dolled up with a nice new permanent, doing fancywork. Just the other day, however, I received the greatest shock of my life when, as reeve of Wilberforce township, I received a bill charging us with $192 for relief for this man, who had drifted into a city or town where he had been able to pull the wool over the eyes of the authorities. He was a young man, able to do. any kind of work.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: That is what we are up against. Hon. members may laugh. They talk as though this government has not done a thing. The other night I was at a farmers' meeting. One of the farmers said to me, "Have you done a single thing since you went to Ottawa?" He kept repeating his question, asking what we had done. I said, "Well, I shipped your hogs when you got $6.20 for a two-hundred pound hog. You give us a two-hundred pound hog to-day and we will give you S20 or $21 for it. You sold your butter fat for 15, 18 or 20 cents a pound. Now you can get 38 cents a pound. Has there been no improvement?"

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Who is responsible?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I am not saying who is responsible, but the improvement is there. Hon. members talk about our youth and ask what we are going to do for them. We hear some of the speakers shout, "Are you going to let them starve?" as though nothing had been done for them. What was done under the youth training scheme? Some six hundred girls were given training, and every one of those girls walked into a job. We had seven girls come to Ottawa from Pembroke to take that course; they all found work. We had

some fifty boys take the engineering course at Haileybury, and every one stepped into a job. There you have it, yet you say we are doing nothing, that we are letting people starve.
The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) talked about the terrible condition of the west; he suggested that we should create $500,000,000 of new money and lend it out. What ruined the west but too much credit? It not only ruined the west; it ruined a good deal of the east as well. They got our money-

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman does not wish to be unfair. I did not mention the west at all, as he will see if he reads my speech.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I listened to the hon. member when he was referring to the west. He spoke of farmers who once were able to write cheques for three thousand, five thousand or ten thousand dollars but who could not borrow any money at all now; and he was suggesting that the farmers of the west were suffering from lack of credit. I say that what the farmers of the west suffered from most was too much credit, and I think if the hon. member wanted to be honest he would agree that it was too much credit that ruined the farmers of western Canada. I remember that in his speech he mentioned some farmer who had five thousand lambs on which he was going to lose money. If the farmer raised those five thousand lambs how could he have a loss on them? On the other hand if that farmer bought the five thousand lambs he was a speculator; if the price went down and he lost money he was a gambler, and he was taking his chance. So I do not see any point in that argument.
There is one angle of this question that I do not think has been touched upon at all. What about the taxpayer? We have spoken of almost everything else. Nearly every speaker advocates the expenditure of money, but I want to put in a word for the taxpayer. We have to give that man consideration. If you can reduce his taxes by even a small amount you will be doing something real for him. One of the greatest burdens on this country to-day is the burden of taxation. When you talk about loading this burden of relief on the federal government you are simply suggesting that the municipalities that kept off relief should turn in now and pay the bills of the municipalities that got themselves in a mess with relief. Personally I am inclined to think that the people who were foolish enough to land themselves in a mess of that nature should themselves find a way

Relief and Agricultural Distress
of getting out from under. The farmers have to pay their share of this eight per cent sales tax and most other federal taxes; that is where the money comes from. That federal tax hits everybody, the hired man, the hired girl and everybody else. No one escapes it. Some of us may escape a provincial or municipal tax, but we cannot escape the federal tax. We ought to keep in mind when we advocate the expenditure of money that we are hitting the pocket of every wage-earner and taxpayer in this dominion. I am in favour of the minister continuing with the program started last year. Naturally it is an experiment, but to my way of thinking it has proven successful. I believe that these plans, carried on in conjunction with the provinces or by the dominion government alone, have proven successful.
Perhaps I may be accused of hitting the taxpayer myself when I ask the minister to consider the improvement of the trans-Canada highway between North Bay and Pembroke. This section of the trans-Canada highway is as important as any other in Canada. It leads to the home of the famous quintuplets and it makes possible a saving of five hundred miles to people travelling from the eastern to the western states, or vice versa. This section is now a gravel road, but it should have a surface of some kind. I am not prepared to suggest that it should be made a cement highway, but something should be done to provide a more suitable surface. Perhaps a tar penetration surface could be put on which would be serviceable for five, ten or fifteen years. We would thus get away from the present high maintenance costs and the dust which is so troublesome. I believe this work would be in the interests of the dominion, particularly as a great portion of our tourist traffic passes over this route.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I ever become wealthy I am going to put up prizes for the most patient men in the country, and when I do, I am sure they will be won by the prime ministers and the members of any cabinet. During this session and for the last twelve years I have seen prime ministers and members of the cabinet put on the grill for weeks at a time when they have been endeavouring to explain certain situations. After answering the same question a thousand times, I have seen them get up very patiently and with a smile on their countenances answer it again. I was surprised this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) accuse the Minister of Labour of not giving the required informations to the committee and of not having brought down his program
more quickly. This is surprising when we consider that during the present session a certain group in this house used up nearly three weeks of our time on a new monetary philosophy. I do not say that in any disparaging way, but I think the record should be kept straight.
I want to compliment the Minister of Labour upon the wonderful work he has done in the three sessions he has been at the head of the Department of Labour. I feel perfectly free to do this. I was a neighbour of the former Minister of Labour, the Hon. Mr. Gordon, and I always took advantage of every opportunity to compliment him also upon the work he accomplished during the abnormal times through which we were passing. I never doubted for one minute the sincerity of the former prime minister when during the election of 1930 he thought he could cure unemployment. At that time we thought this problem was not deeply rooted and was possible of solution.
Before I proceed any further I want to say to the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou) that he was extremely unfair this afternoon when he asked the Minister of Labour what had been done for the west. There is no sectionalism as far as the problems of the west are concerned. I remember last fall when the people in my section of the country were asked to give clothing, vegetables and fruits to the people of the west. No matter in what position of life they were, every one dug down gladly to give all they possibly could to this fine section of the population of Canada. What has been done for the west during the present session? Something like $35,000,000 or $40,000,000 has been voted. Is that nothing? When that vote was asked, there was not a single word of criticism. Not a single member rose in his place and criticized this item. Why? Because we realized the dire necessity of the people in the west and the need for that money. I know the members of this house are ready to	rise as	one	person and	voteeverything necessary for the maintenance of that fine section of our country, if circumstances warrant our so doing again. It is true that no matter what this parliament may vote, this problem cannot be solved, to some extent, I grant, until the west	has	good crops sellingat reasonable	prices.	At	the present	timethe people of	the west in	the drought	areas
are existing with the barest essentials of life. Their household furniture, their farm implements and their homes all need to be rehabilitated. Again I repeat it is unfair for any member of this parliament at this time

Relief and Agricultural Distress
to state to the Minister of Labour and to the government that nothing has been done so far as the west is concerned.
Any one who takes the trouble to study world history will realize that unemployment has existed since the dawn of civilization. In the early days thousands of young men were kept under arms simply because they could not be fruitfully employed. We must not overlook what is happening in Europe at the present time. We must not overlook the reason why hundreds of thousands, yes, millions of men are being kept in military service. I ask hon. members to consider the reply made three years ago by Hitler to the Prime Minister of France. France was concerned about the number of men that Germany had under arms, and Hitler replied that this was done in order to keep them off the unemployment relief rolls. That may not be the principal reason why these men are under arms, but I think it is one of the reasons.
This is the situation we had in Canada prior to 1930. We always have had seasonal employment in this country. In my section and in practically all other sections we have had tens of thousands of young men employed during the winter months in lumbering operations. These men will be unemployed for one, two or three months until the driving of logs and mill operations commence in the spring. However, during this period considerable agricultural work is carried on, and a number of men are able to obtain employment in the navigation operations on our great lakes. This problem is not a new one as far as we are concerned, and we get these changes every, season.
It is all very well for people to impute sinister motives in connection with those who are wealthy people; we call them big shots and so on; speak of their greed, their intolerance, etc.; but the great majority of these people are true Canadians and their hearts are with the working men and labourers. The same thing can be said of most of our people; their hearts are in the proper place, and they will do everything in their power to alleviate suffering. At the same time there have been cases where the labourers and farmers have sinned also, with all the other classes. It is all very well for a member to mention individual cases of having met men in dire circumstances. I could mention thousands of such cases in my own constituency, even in the rural sections where they have been receiving relief for several years. I have also received several letters from farmers saying that their lot is improving. They have been selling their milk at reasonable prices and last year they made some

money on their pulpwood and cattle, but you cannot build up a case for the nation on individual cases.
I might cite a sad case that came under my own experience last year, and that will illustrate what I have said. Last year during the Easter recess, on Good Friday, a young farmer with a family of seven came and told me that he had received $32 on April 1, 1937, and he said his relief was all gone and he wanted some more. I telephoned the relief officer in Cochrane and told him that this man had to receive more relief because his family was near starvation. That, as I say, was on Good Friday. Sad to relate, on Saturday night this man asked me to bail him out as he had spent all the money on booze instead of on his family, and he had been arrested for drunkenness.
All classes of our people have sinned, and therefore it is the duty of every one of us, no matter to what party he belongs, or on which side of the house he sits, or what is his place in society, to put his whole strength behind the minister and the government in helping to bring about better conditions. We are just as humane and charitable as any other men, and how unfair it is for the member of Winnipeg North Centre to rise in his place this afternoon and accuse the Minister of Labour very bitterly, saying he had done nothing for the unemployed; that he was not trying to find the solution for unemployment. I say this in all sincerity because from 1930 to 1935 I sat in opposition on the other side of the house, and I did not criticize bitterly the government of the day and their employment policies because I knew it was a very deep problem. I believe the first duty of every member of parliament is to second the efforts of the Minister of Labour, and I hope that from now on it will be possible to discuss in this house this great problem with the sole desire to help in solving it by suggestions and constructive criticism. It is a problem that is facing not only Canada but the whole civilized world. Look to the country to the south of us, where billions and bilhons of dollars have been spent for the relief of unemployment, and the sad truth is "that at present unemployment in that country is more rampant than it was two years ago. Europe has just the same problem, and all of Europe found that the only way to help in solving it was to put the young men from eighteen to twenty-one years of age in the army. Surely we do not want to do that in Canada. We want to help our youth; but we do not want to develop in them the militaristic spirit; we want them to grow up to be good Canadians,

Relief and Agricultural Distress
and therefore I say it behooves every member of this house, no matter on which side he sits, to be constructive in his approach to that all important problem. How easy it would be for any one of us to go outside this house, hold a public meeting on Sparks street, for example, agitate the people by telling them not to be satisfied with the present government, and urge them to destroy the present order of things! But would that be good Canadianism? Would it be patriotic? No. My duty when I see misery is in my own humble way and to the best of my ability to help relieve it, and if we all put our shoulders to the wheel I have no doubt that by an intelligent, united effort we shall get out of our present situation.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: You have the majority.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: A few moments ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre read the message that was delivered to the Canadian people by the Prime Minister during the last election, and I heard a member of the social credit group say that it was a dream. But it was not a dream. It was given in all sincerity, just as I believe the leader of the government who was elected in 1930 spoke in all sincerity; just as I believe the premier of Alberta spoke in all sincerity to the people of that province in 1935 when he was elected premier. He told the people of Alberta that he was going to solve all their problems; that he was going to pay social credit dividends of $25 a month and more, and I believe that he was sincere. The electors of Alberta gave him a huge majority, and at that time he told the people of the province not to worry about the rest of Canada, or Scotland; that Mr. Douglas had said that social credit might not be put into practice within the boundaries of the province, but that he, that is, Mr. Aber-hart, could do this. But after over two years in office, with all his sincerity, which I do not doubt at all, has he been able to put social credit principles into practice in that province? Is there not unemployment in Alberta? There have been bad crops there, which have no doubt contributed to a great extent to unemployment in that province, but I say that with all his sincerity, and with all his big, solid majority behind him, the premier of Alberta has not been able to implement, the promises he made during the election of 1935.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The Liberals disallowed all our legislation. There was no doubt of the application of social credit in 1935.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
There is no question .that the social credit party had a large
majority behind it in Alberta, and I do not say that in any critical spirit. I mention it merely because one of the members of the social credit group this afternoon said, alluding to the message delivered by the Prime Minister immediately after the election of 1935, that it was a dream. Was it a dream, then, what the premier of Alberta told the people of that province in the fall of the same year, 1935? No; I do not want to believe it. I want to believe implicitly in his sincerity; but he was not able to fulfil all his promises; he did not fulfil even one. The moment one assumes the responsibility of office, one finds that it is not so easy to do in practice what one advocated in theory.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Does that not prove that sincerity is not enough; that sincerity alone will not solve any problem? Sincerity will not abolish poverty.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: It is obvious that sincerity is necessary because the basic principle of any society is charity, and sincerity is an essential part of it.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: You must have sincerity plus direction.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Oh, yes. I have something to say about the sincerity of the party of my hon. friend, and I shall take a few minutes to speak of it now. I wish his party could have the responsibility of office for one or two years because it would sober them up. We on this side of the house are just the same as hon. gentlemen opposite; our hearts are bleeding for the suffering people of this country.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: You have the authority; what more do you want?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Your only solution is
to change the monetary system, but the monetary system is only one of the factors which we have to consider before we can have improved conditions. It is veiy easy to criticize when one is in opposition. I was in opposition lor five successive years. While some members may have gone too far in their theories, once your party gets into power you have to consider all the factors involved plus the governmental responsibilities, and I believe that all governments in this dominion, no matter what their political stripe, have at heart the welfare of the people, the human and the social factors. I say again that it is extremely unfair to build up on individual cases a case that will apply to the whole nation.
I want to compliment the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) upon his

Relief and Agricultural Distress
logical speech this afternoon. Democracy is before the bar of judgment in Canada, and I want to give this warning, that if the parties in this house address themselves simply to overdoing each other at election time in rash statements and in promises that would never be fulfilled, it will be the surest sign of the doom of our democracy. In the last election, in northern Ontario, I went over every section of my constituency and told the people that I was opposed to direct relief. I told them that the sooner we got rid of it, the better it would be for our country, that we had to find employment for our people, and that direct relief was deteriorating, if not destroying, the moral fibre of the nation. It was a sad spectacle to see people of another political faith getting up on the same platform as we were on, and saying that if they were elected they would not do like the Liberals are trying to do at the present time; they would enlarge direct relief; they would give more. I say that sort of thing is the surest way to destroy democracy in Canada. We cannot afford to be demagogues, dreamers, Utopians and radicals; we must be good, practical Canadians.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
We cannot
afford to sleep, either.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
To sleep? Does the
hon. member imply by that that I have been sleeping more than he has? Does he imply that this government has bean asleep more than his group?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: It has been put to sleep.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Some days that hon.
members of a certain group have been speaking we may have been almost put to sleep for a good many hours. I want this situation to be dealt with fairly. I want to be a practical man. I ask hon. members, If they were occupying the position of the present Minister of Labour, what would they do? Can they doubt his sincerity, his industry, his knowledge of the social order and his desire to remedy social problems? If not, they should be willing to cooperate with him. It is not a political appeal that I am making at the present time. I appeal to hon. members to face and to try to find a solution for the greatest difficulty we have to meet.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The hon. member
has told us that the hearts of his friends are bleeding for the sufferings of the unemployed. I mentioned that poverty was the cause of their trouble. Will he tell us what unemployed and suffering people are suffering from except a lack of money?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Dividends.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: None of the experts who support the system which the hon. member recommends, has been able to explain it.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I ask, What are these poor people suffering from except lack of money?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I am not here to say that the present monetary system is perfect. Perhaps it will have to be radically amended. But I repeat that the monetary problem is not the only question we are facing at the present time.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Then what are the other problems?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Surely the hon. member must know more about human needs than to ask that question. What would he do, for instance, in the case of a returned man I know? Money will not cure all the ills of the present time. I have a good many returned men in my section. One I have in mind has two wooden legs; he suffers every minute of his life, day and night. Does the hon. member contend that if he had social credit money in his pocket, that would be sufficient to cure him?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

And we are not going to cure all our ills by the issue of money by means of the printing press, which is simply uncontrolled inflation.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

speechtext: That was an age of scarcity. This is an age of abundance. To-day we are suffering from overproduction. In Rome they were suffering from scarcity. How can the hon. member dr. w a comparison between the two? It is absurd.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The hon. member is
entitled to his own theories, but I say that this is no age of plenty. What would happen in the hon. member's own province if he had nothing but his coal and his wheat to live upon? How far would he go with that? Practically all that is produced in Alberta is wheat and oil and coal. Supposing you have to make a living with those resources, nationally and individually, what sort of existence would be possible? Obviously you must have intercourse with the rest of the world. You cannot get away from that fact. The "age of plenty" is only relative. The man who will say that we have solved the world's problems of production can say so only because he does not wish to take the trouble to study the situation. He does not want to study the world situation. It is true that to a great extent we have shown that we can produce the things we want, and I am willing to admit that there is probably no clear demarcation between the things we regard as necessities
Relief and Agricultural Distress

and the comforts and luxuries of life; but no one will make me believe that these things can be had unless one is willing to work. In this world you cannot get something for nothing. That is the law of nature. It may be broken; it may be evaded, but the man who is not willing to work for a living is not entitled to a living, while opportunities must be given to those who want to work.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: What is the man doing for a living who receives dividends?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
In this country one has to fight every inch of the way. I come from a pioneer section and I know whereof I speak. It was settled by splendid people, a number of whom came from the other side. In my section we have to fight every inch of the way, whether our occupation is agricultural, or commercial, or mining, or industrial. I3 it any easier in Alberta? As to making it easy in all sections of the country, if hon. members visualize the situation as realists, not as men who have lost all sense of proportion, they will realize that there is no plenty in this world unless one fights and struggles for it, and that production can be brought forward only by human labour and intelligence.
That is all I wish to say at the moment. I should like to say a few words when the estimates on the back to the land movement are presented. I do not believe in simple formulae for solving the problems of the world at the present time. There is no use in talking about ending unemployment and having prosperity in our midst in Canada, or in any other section of the civilized world, unless we find it possible to render comfortable, if not prosperous, the rural population who in this land and in all others are, after all, the primary producers. In this, in my viewpoint, lies, to a large extent, the solution of unemployment.

speechtext: What bearing has this on the bill?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

I am discussing a remark made by the hon. member for Lethbridge in the course of the debate last evening. The effect of the newspaper item and the reference I have just given as quoted from Hansard is that there are 500 people in Yarmouth being fed at a soup kitchen, or 500 people in Yarmouth who stroll along to get a bowl of soup. I want to tell the committee that that is not a fact. There is not in Yarmouth, which is a part of my constituency, any soup kitchen to which 500 people stroll along to get a bowl of soup. When the leader of the social credit group says, " I am more concerned with having members in the house know about existing conditions," I am sorry for his group if they base all their representations on information of this kind. I contend that any member of this house who makes statements should at least be sufficiently informed to know whether they are true or not. It is all very well to read a letter and to profess to be only the means of representing facts in this house; he should strive to be accurate. I resent false representations being made about the people I represent. We are having difficulties enough without being slandered in this way to bolster up the aspirations of what we might call superpoliticians trying to picture conditions that do not exist. That will do no good to any group or member or constituency, nor will it do any good to Canada as a whole. I know of no soup kitchen in Yarmouth where-and this is the part that stings-500 people stroll along for a bowl of soup.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, March 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) for concurrence in the second report of the special committee appointed to investigate farm implement prices, presented to the house on the 8th of April, 1937.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
In rising to continue this debate I wonder whether the remarks I shall have to make will meet with as much enthusiasm as the remarks we have listened to during the debate on the unemployment relief resolution. What I have to say may not be interesting to every hon. member, but to me the question of cheaper agricultural implements is of very great importance. In commencing I want to review briefly the question of the tariff on agricultural implements.
Going back to 1930, when the Liberal administration left office, we enjoyed at that time a very low tariff on agricultural implements, perhaps the lowest on record, only six per cent on binders and mowers. When the Conservative government came into office in 1930, the tariff was raised to the highest rate
on record, namely, a flat rate of twenty-five per cent, including cream separators, which previously had been free. When the Conservatives left office in 1935 and were succeeded by the present administration, true to Liberal policy the tariff was reduced and cut to seven and a half per cent.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: What about the prices of the implements?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
I ^rould ask the right hon. leader of the opposition to let me continue. Perhaps, before I conclude my remarks, I shall have something to say as to prices of implements.
The present tariff of seven and a half per cent is the lowest on record, if excise taxes and some other imposts put on through the regulations of the revenue department are not taken into account. But in the face of this reduction in the tariff we find the implement companies increasing their prices in 1936, and again in 1938. To me this looks like a challenge to the parliament of Canada. What are we going to do about it?
Briefly I wish to review the progress of this matter in the house. On March 2, 1936, an order of the house was passed for an immediate inquiry. At the end of that session the committee reported and suggested that the inquiry be continued by a smaller committee at the next session. On February 1, 1937, the government moved the appointment of a special committee. That committee carried on an investigation throughout the session of 1937; and the report was submitted on April 8 of that year, but at the suggestion of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) it was not concurred in but left over until the present session. On March 11 of this year the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston) moved concurrence, after six weeks of the session had passed. The debate was adjourned on March 11 by the hon. member for Kamour-aska (Mr. Bouchard) and continued on March 15 and adjourned by myself on the same day. Thus it will be seen that it is well over two years since parliament started action. To me this has been a horrible example of how not to treat a question of such vital importance to the agricultural industry of this country.
Now I am back to the position which I occupied at eleven p.m. on March 15. Before the house adjourned on that date, I had pointed out the disparity between the farmer's dollar received for his products and what he had to pay for farm implements. I took, for example, the prices of beef cattle at the Winnipeg stock yards, for 1913, 1920, 1926, 1932 and 1936, and I took for the purpose of comparison two-

implements, a walking plough and a binder. As I stated at that time, the committee took the year 1913 as a normal year when the farmer's dollar bore a reasonable relation to the prices he had to pay for his products. I was able to show that in 1913 we could exchange 300 pounds of beef cattle for a walking plough, whereas in 1932 it required 700 pounds to make the same exchange. In 1913 we could purchase a binder for 2,600 pounds; but in 1932 it would cost us 6,100 pounds, approximately two and a half times
as much. Continuing the thread of my argument, I -have a companion table giving a comparison of the farmer's dollar in terms of wheat instead of cattle. It shows the same list of implements as used on that occasion. The walking plough, for example, which in 1913 we could buy for the price of twenty-five bushels of wheat, in 1932 would cost fifty-six bushels. A binder which in 1913 was equivalent to 193 bushels of wheat, in 1932 required 500 bushels. The following table gives other examples:

These tables are a true indication of what is wrong with agriculture, showing the fluctuation in the prices of the farmer's products sold on the world market compared with the stabilized prices he has to pay for his implements of production sold in a protected market. This condition must be rectified before agriculture can be put upon a substantial basis.
Leaving farm implements for the moment, let me turn to cream separators. This question was discussed on former occasions. I remember a speech made by my Liberal friend the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald). He defended the twenty-five per cent tariff on cream separators. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) replied, and his speech was, in my opinion, a fine exposition of the necessity for the removal of this duty. To me it seemed unanswerable; but another Liberal friend, the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) was undaunted, and he defended the twenty-five per cent tariff on cream separators. It is true that these two hon. members were invited to cross the floor of the house and join the Conservative party. I wonder myself whether they are not in the wrong pew.
When the motion for concurrence was introduced, the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) both protested and suggested that the report be returned to the committee for more evidence, saying that insufficient evidence had been taken in regard to cream separators. But if one looks at the report one finds at least four pages of evidence in regard to cream

separators. Four manufacturing companies as well as a mail order house were examined: International Harvester Company, Massey -Harris, De Laval and McLeod's Limited of Winnipeg, besides the Cockshutt Plow Company whose evidence, being confidential, was not used. So I maintain we certainly had sufficient evidence to warrant the committee in bringing in the recommendation that cream separators should be placed on the free list. The mail order house in reply to a letter stated that they had been able to place on the market a separator called the Melotte with a capacity of 600 pounds, for $59.25 at Winnipeg. That is the Melotte, which is a good machine, as anyone will agree who knows anything about separators. The Economy King, with a capacity of 600 pounds, was placed on the market at $54 at Winnipeg. At the same time the International Harvester Company were selling their 600 separator at $107.58, and the committee ascertained that the cost of that separator at the factory was $41.70. This would be about the same as the cost of the Melotte and the Economy King, because the McLeod people were satisfied with a twenty-five per cent mark-up over the cost price. We found that the Massey-Harris company were charging $97.92 for their separator. We could not ascertain the cost of that implement because the company could not produce figures that would give us an idea of what the cost would be. The De Laval people were charging $108.77 for their separator comparable with the McLeod separator at $59.25.

Farm Implements Committee Report
We found also that the De Laval people could buy their smaller separators, under 500 pounds, in Sweden and import them, paying the duty, at a price which enabled the company to offer the separators for sale for less than the price at which they could be manufactured in Canada. Surely this is evidence that it is uneconomical to manufacture these machines in this country. These separators cost $13.05 in Sweden, and they were sold in Canada for $44.50 including the duty of twenty-five per cent. When the higher protection was put on cream separators, the McLeod people admitted that they could not do business, and they withdrew from the field. After the competition was elminated we find that last year the International Harvester company raised the price of their cream separator another $11. To-day their separator is selling in Winnipeg at $118.50, which is an outrageous price for the implement that must be turned by the farmer's wife, or his fourteen or fifteen year old girl after she comes home from school, or his boy, in order to grind out perhaps three or four dollars a week in order to keep the family in food and clothing. I claim that this duty on cream separators is protection gone mad, and I think it is a terrible reflection upon the mentality of those who imposed the duty.
Now I want to return to farm implements. In the first part of my speech I stated that both farmers and machine companies had suffered grievously during the years of depression, but the machine companies did not suffer to the same extent as did the farmers. I have before me the financial statements from the evidence given before the special committee. I find that the capital invested in the International Harvester company in Canada is $39,000,000, and that the profits during the ten year period under review amounted to $24,500,000. They earned approximately six and a half per cent over all, after providing for a pension fund, bonuses to employees and taxes of all kinds. I asked the president of the company, Mr. Morrison, if he did not think that was a pretty high earning rate, amd what he thought would be about a proper earning rate for money. His reply was eight per cent over all; in other words, they wanted eight per cent even after the taxes were paid. So I say that in regard to this company the increase in the price of their farm implements in 1936 certainly was not justified.
Now we come to John Deere and Company. Their capital invested in Canada amounted to $16,000,000. They showed a loss of $1,000,000 in Canada, but if the profits retained in the United States on account of customs regulations
had been included the profit would have been $8,000,000 over the ten year period, showing a five per cent return on the investment. Then I come to Frost and Wood and the Cockshutt Plow Company. The invested capital could not be ascertained, but the total sales in Canada amounted to $45,600,000 and their export sales to $7,772,000. These two companies showed a net profit of $20,760, so they also operated without loss during this ten year period which included the most trying years Canada has ever experienced.
There is a different story in regard to the Massey-Harris company. This is a great Canadian concern of which every true Canadian is proud. They have factories not only in Canada but also in England, South Africa, France, Belgium, Denmark and Germany, as well as two factories in the United States. Between 1926 and 1935 the losses of this company amounted to $15,000,000. But, Mr. Speaker, prior to that they had huge profits. I think it only fair to the people of Canada that they should know something about the profits made by this company in earlier years. This is taken from the evidence given before the special committee. The company had its inception in 1891, with the merging of the Massey and Harris interests. The paid-up capital of the company at its inception was approximately $3,500,000, of which $300,000 was paid in cash and the remainder given in exchange for the assets of the constituent firms. From 1891 to 1912 this original capitalization of $3,500,000 plus $1,000,000 additional cash capital received in 1911 enabled the company to return the following

What I wish to say will take only about three or four minutes of the time oif the committee. I desire to refer to some of the remarks that were made by the right hon. leader of the opposition on Tuesday evening last. He was referring to what I had said on the evening of Friday, April 8. and this is what he said, as reported on page 2277 of Hansard:
Right here may I point out that the other evening the hon. member for Peterborough West in this very chamber asked the members of the committee to believe that the United States authorities had given their approval to the construction of this bridge.
Further down on the same page he said:
That statement was calculated to do just one thing and nothing else-to leave the impression with the house that the United States had agreed.

When I was elected by the people whom I have the honour to represent in this house, I accepted my duties with a keen sense of duty, obligation and responsibility, and I should like the members of this committee and house to understand that at no time do I impute or intend to impute motives that are not consistent with the facts.

Mr. Chairman, I know of no reason why, because one happens to be a member of the House of Commons of Canada, he should be traduced by those who are outside this house. The late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, as leader of this house, on two occasions held that the privileges of parliament were not to be lightly disregarded, and when a member of the opposition with whom his relations could not be said to be cordial, the late Sir George Foster, directed attention to observations that had been made reflecting upon him in the house and made a motion, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, although the person accused was his own friend, saw that he was brought to the bar of the house to apologize for what he had said. The privileges of parliament are not of to-day's making. They represent centuries of accumulated tradition and history, and if men in the discharge of their duty are to be charged with offences and traduced in the public press by those who do not see eye to eye with them, then of course the institution itself is going to suffer. The custody of the reputation of the house is not in my hands, but I direct attention to the facts.
The other evening I directed attention, as was my duty, to the fact that because an attack had been made against this house, alleging that we had not passed legislation as rapidly as we should have, I thought it was my duty to look into this measure, and I did so and gave to this committee the benefit of the information which I had obtained-not all of it but in part-because when this house is charged with having neglected its duties or with having been overzealous in its efforts to discharge them, it seemed to me but fitting that the legislation which has been the subject of controversy should be scrutinized.
I am bound to say that I have not been able to ascertain who the incorporators of this bridge company are. So far as I can ascertain, they are not even people of substance. But that has nothing to do with the question. The question which I presented
Niagara Falls Bridge

for the consideration of the committee had only to deal with the legislation as such, and I pointed out that in most bills of this kind it has been provided that when the dominion acts it shall not exercise its powers until similar legislation has been passed by the state of New York, or by the adjoining state, whether it be Michigan or New York, and, if necessary, approved by the United States of America as a nation. I point out that that provision is to be found in the very section which we are now considering, and I direct the attention of the committee very seriously to these words:
. . . but the company shall not commence the actual construction of the said bridge nor exercise any of the powers hereunder, until an act of congress of the United States or other competent authority in the United States of America has been passed authorizing or approving such bridging of the said river.
That is the usual clause. That is where, as the hon. gentleman in charge of this bill will say, the legislation usually stops. But this bill went further. It has this extraordinary provision:
But the company may, in the meantime acquire the lands, submit their plans to the governor in council, and do all things authorized by this act.
I venture to point out-and I believe it to be my duty to do so-that that is a contradiction in terms; that you cannot approbate and reprobate. In the one instance the powers are to be exercised only when the appropriate authority in the United States has authorized the company to construct a bridge from the United States territory to the middle of the stream; that is, the middle of the Niagara river, which is the boundary line between Canada and the United States.
Just here it might be well to point out that this legislation has a history. I wonder if it is known to all hon. members that this company under another name has had a bridge in that place for nearly forty years. One of the very earliest bridges to cross the Niagara was built by this company under another name, that of the Buffalo railway company. They did so under authority from the United States and then came to this parliament and obtained in 1900 legislation which enabled them to complete the structure. They also had a railway line. Those who live in that locality are far more familiar with the matter than I am. but I have taken the trouble to look it up a little in view of what has occurred. I find that a short time ago the province of Ontario took steps to acquire the scenic railway, as it is called, and there was an arbitration, the net .result of which was that the province or the

park authorities have now been called upon to pay something like $1,072,587. In the journals of the Ontario house of assembly, at page 229. I find this:
Bank loan (note) (for International railway award), $1,072,587.
(The costs in connection with the award are not included in the above amount; they amount to $136,150.09 and have been paid out of the commission's funds.)
I am indebted to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) for a copy of the journals from which that information was taken. The feeling against the International company, apparently, has been considerable, by reason of the fact that this very large sum of a million dollars had to be paid. The provincial minister of highways, Mr. Mc-Questen. came to this house and, speaking before, the committee, said they were going to pass a statute dealing with bridges; he is also reported to have said that "it would make one more hurdle to cross." And so they did pass a statute with respect to bridges, aimed clearly at the International, for the purpose of preventing the reconstruction of this bridge. That is not a matter in which I have any concern; it is only a matter of passing historical interest. The International company, its former name, the Buffalo railway, having been changed by act of our parliament as well as that of the legislature of Ontario, did operate this bridge and this scenic railway for many years. The scenic railway has been acquired by the appropriate park authority for the province of Ontario under the circumstances to which I have alluded. There remains the question of rebuilding a structure which was destroyed by an act of God. The ice jam took the bridge out. The International people at once arranged for the reconstruction of their bridge, and plans were prepared to that end. A bill was introduced into the legislature of the state of New York- one bill in the assembly and the other in the senate. They bear date February 18, 1938, and they have to do with the construction from the United States side of this bridge. But that bill did not pass. I hold in my hand a statement signed by Senator W. H. Lee of the state of New York, who resides at Lock-port, in which he refers to the conference which was held for the purpose of determining what action should be taken. These are the terms in which he writes:

That statement, it will be seen, is not new. As a matter of fact, the conference took place as long ago as February, and at it the governor made it perfectly clear what his course was. Now I point out to the committee that this legislation had its origin in the United States. They first granted the power to construct the bridge. The promoters then came to this parliament and obtained from it the power to connect up with the bridge, on the Canadian side. As I have pointed out, in the course of years they have acquired much property. They have this scenic railway, which has been sold. They have the approaches at both ends of the bridge; highways lead down to this bridge, and there were many of the amenities of travel established at both ends of the structure before it was destroyed. Also there are people with homes in the locality and such stores and shops as are always found in such localities. The value placed on the property owned by this bridge company is 8500.000. This proposal is to construct a bridge at another point, which involves the acquisition of land for approaches, the diversion of highways, and the erection and construction of the amenities that have now been provided in connection with the International bridge. That is the position.
So far as what I said the other evening is concerned, and which the committee might care to read-I am not going to reread it-I pointed out that if the bridge cannot be constructed until such time as the United States appropriate authority gives permission to build from the United States side to the centre of the stream, how could we authorize a company that might never function-because the bill itself says it can function only if, as and when the United States authorities authorize a company to build from their shore to the middle of the stream-to acquire real estate
and file plans for the approval of the governor general in council? Of what bridge? It is only when the two have amalgamated into a single bridge that we have a structure, and as the Minister of Transport said the other evening, it does not require an act of parliament to enable you to prepare plans for a bridge, but to prepare plans and ask for approval of them when there is no such thing as a bridge authorized, is something that I cannot understand.
Just why these last words are placed in that section I would ask the committee to determine for itself. But in view of the fact that the section dealt with the acquisition of real estate I said it could mean only one thing, the creation of a real estate boom at the point where the bridge was to be built and where a community was to be built around it-the little shops that sell fruit and confectionery and cards and things of that sort. Of course, anyone with any practical knowledge of affairs knows exactly what happens the very moment it is mooted that a new structure of this sort is under contemplation, just as in connection with the Peace bridge there were activities in that locality, and as there are activities in every locality where the construction of a bridge is contemplated.
I gave notice on the order paper that I would move an amendment that the words after the word "river" be struck out in order that this legislation might be consistent with other legislation that we have passed on previous occasions. Whenever we exercise a power that is limited, by geographical and international facts, to a point in the centre of a stream, the building of the bridge results only from the United States authorities authorizing a similar structure to be carried on from that side of the border to the centre. The two then amalgamate and you have the completed structure. That is what took place in connection with the Peace bridge. I could name many other bridges of the same kind, including the Sarnia structure. That did not cross into the state of New York; I believe it was the state of Michigan. Be that as it may, I hardly think it would be just the right thing for legislators to authorize the building of a structure by a company which is permitted to exercise its fuctions only when something else has been done in another country, and at the same time authorize it to engage in a real estate boom. That is what it means, and that is the point to which I directed attention.
There are other matters to which I might direct attention, and I am going to refer at once to one of them. The hon. member for

Peterborough West (Mr. Duffus) said, as did a gentleman who is not a member of this house, that the province of Ontario is suffering. Mr. Chairman, see what ensues from the following statements: (1) The legislature of the state of New York has declined to authorize the construction of this bridge at this time; (2) the legislature of the state of New York has prorogued for the year- you may have seen that in the New York Times ten days ago. There can be, therefore, no bridge authorized this year, and we have nothing to do with that; that is a matter -which the state of New York has determined. And the condition imposed in this very bill is that the powers hereby conferred shall not be exercised until such time as the state of New York or the congress of the United States authorizes the construction of a bridge. That, I say, completely answers everything that has been said about the province of Ontario losing anything.
How can the province of Ontario lose anything when the legislature of the state of New York has risen for the year and has declined to take action? How can it be so when the condition appears in the very bill that the promoter puts before us, that "the company shall not commence the actual construction of the said bridge nor exercise any of the powers hereunder, until an act of the congress of the United States or other competent authority in the United States of America has been passed authorizing or approving such bridging of the said river." There is a distinct and clear recognition, a recognition which has been found in all our international legislation, that there must be joint action in order to bridge an international stream, and that we cannot confer powers to be exercised by any company beyond the middle of a stream. Surely we do not propose to make ourselves absurd by authorizing such action to be taken until such time as the United States authorities have authorized the construction of the bridge from their end as well.
Why the hon. member who is promoting the bill has added the words he has, I confess I do not know, although I have looked for some reason for them. Let me read the language once more:
But the company may in the meantime acquire the lands, submit their plans to the governor in council and do all filings authorized by this act.
"Do all things authorized by this act," notwithstanding that three lines before that it is said that "the company shall not commence the actual construction of the said bridge nor exercise any of the powers hereunder,

until an act of congress of the United States or other competent authority in the United States of America has been passed," and so on.
I put this to the committee. I have no feeling at all in the matter, despite what has been said; because, after all, I have in this exactly the same interest that I had in the legislation of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) regarding the Restigouche company. In that connection I pointed out certain things; the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) saw my point and the bill was amended accordingly. I had no particular interest in that matter, nor have I any particular interest in this, and I have been too long in public life to be concerned about attacks made against me or this committee. I do say, however, that we cannot declare in a statute that certain persons shall not exercise any of the powers conferred by the bill until the United States takes joint action to build a bridge to the centre of the stream, and at the same time, two lines further on, declare that they may do all the things authorized by this act; that they may start to buy land and to file plans-plans of what? Plans of a bridge. But there is no bridge authorized to cross the stream; so far, it stops at the centre of it. It may be that something is left out; it may be that hon. gentlemen have confused two things; and all that I suggested, in the notice of amendment which I gave, was that the section be amended by striking out all the words after the word "river," which would have this effect, that the legislation would not be contradictory in the last five lines, and would be at any rate consistent with our legal as well as our international position; for having said, as we may say, that we are not doing anything beyond our legal powers, we have gone as far as we can. I submit that we should remove any possible thought that any action taken here, even if we kill this bill, would deprive the province of Ontario of any revenue, or the Dominion of Canada of any tourists. The state of New York has seen fit not to give its approval, not to create a company and what is more, the legislature of the state has risen for the year. It follows, therefore, that as far as this bill is concerned it is a dead measure during the period which intervenes until such time as that legislature has acted.
I confess it is disagreeable to have these discussions and to be attacked in the beautiful language that always characterizes the utterances of the gentleman who used it, perhaps somewhat out of keeping with the long traditions of an ancient province. To say that
