something is a damnable lie is not calculated to enhance the reputation of the person who said it, or yet respect for the institution which he represents. I think I can say that at least. The facts are as I have stated them. I have nothing to withdraw, nothing to explain in any sense. What I said is on Hansard; it stands written, printed; and it is strictly in accordance with the facts. The legislation in itself denies the right to construct until the United States has acted, and then it authorizes this company, which has no valid life, to deal in real estate and file plans with the governor in council. It has no authority to build beyond the middle of the stream until the United States has acted. And then it is joint action.
I need hardly say to the right hon. the Prime Minister that it would seem that we can hardly afford to place ourselves in the position in which this legislation would place us with our great neighbour to the south. It assumes that we are to give approval to the building of a bridge in the state of New York. We would not take kindly to the state of New York passing a statute authorizing the government of that state to approve plans of a bridge to be erected in the Dominion of Canada. But this bill says that although you cannot act until the state of New York gives you power, nevertheless, although you have no legal right, no validity to your acts, we are going to let you buy and sell real estate and file plans with the governor in council of a bridge part of which must be in the state of New York. That is the position. I have done my duty by pointing it out. When the hon. member for Peterborough West was speaking the other evening, I asked him if he did not know that this legislation had not been passed. He did not answer the question; but surely when we remember that the minister of highways for Ontario was present at the conference with the governor in February last, it would be difficult for him not to know that the legislature had risen and that no action had been taken with respect to it.
Those are the facts on section 8 to which I have directed attention, and it is only necessary to add that, as pointed out the other evening, the estimate given by the engineer, Colonel Monsarrat, of the cost of the bridge to be erected by the International company is $1,400,000. At the proper time I shall discuss the financial side of this matter; for it is said that the purpose is to give the people a bridge free from tolls. The authorized bond issue is $4,000,000. and if the money were obtained at the lowest rate at which money was obtained for the Peace bridge, it
would involve an annual interest payment of $200,000, apart from sinking fund and without providing for expenses of operation. The files in the department indicate what the earnings of this company have been during all these years. I had an abstract made of some of them which may be useful later on in connection with other sections.
But it is said that the province could not obtain this legislation. All you need do is to turn to the statutes of this dominion in 1931, when the province of Quebec came here and obtained authority to construct a bridge from the Isle of Orleans to the mainland. In that case it was navigable water to be crossed, and they had to secure our authority, which was given by statute, before they could construct that bridge. In the case of this bridge it is not navigable water but international water that is to be bridged, and obviously both countries must join together for the purpose of making action possible. When we have made our act contingent upon the exercise by the other party of their power, and they have not exercised that power and will not now for another year, it seems to me we are doing something very much at variance with the declarations which have been made from time to time in this house with respect to investments and company promotions and the evils that have flowed from such exploitations, unless we take the only step we can with respect to this section and leave it as similar sections have been left in dealing with other companies; namely, providing that the power shall not be exercised unless and until the competent authority in the United States has authorized and empowered a corporation to exercise its powers.

This bill has been under discussion for several weeks, and it is not my purpose to prolong the debate. But after the forensic display to which we have listened from the right hon. leader of the opposition, on the last two sittings on which the bill has been before the committee, I feel that a statement is necessary as to just what is involved in this bill. The motives of the province of Ontario have been impugned, and gratuitous insults have been distributed to whoever has spoken on behalf of the measure.
What are the facts? The Niagara parks commission has expended large sums of money and done splendid work in making the neighbourhood of Niagara Falls a beauty spot and a tourist attraction. This commission now desires to build an entrance to the city from the United States that will be a credit to that city and to the parks commission's
Niagara Falls Bridge

development. The stream to be bridged is an international one; hence in order to do what they wish to do it is necessary for the commissioners to obtain the consent of the federal government and of the proper authority in the United States. Obviously those consents cannot be obtained concurrently; one or the other must be obtained first. It was legally impossible for either the Niagara parks commission or for Ontario as a province to apply in its own name to the federal government for the requisite permission to build.
Quebec did.

That was somewhat different. However, I shall not enter into a discussion about that. The provincial authorities then followed the usual procedure, or what seemed to them to be the usual procedurethey chose five men, connected in one capacity or another with either the parks commission or the province of Ontario. They entered into an agreement with these men that the five men would form a corporation for the purpose of applying to this parliament for the necessary authority, and when the authority had been obtained, to assign their interest in the corporation to the province of Ontario. A private bill was drawn up, and the legal adviser of my department who inspected the bill has advised me that it follows the exact language of the last bill passed by this parliament, and in general follows very closely the language of the bills authorizing the last several international bridges that have been approved by this parliament. The bill was introduced in this parliament, and the province of Ontario sent this government an official letter stating that the incorporators of this company were acting for the province; that their interest would be assigned to the province, and that the province would undertake responsibility for the construction and operation.

bill by members of the committee; for example, the amount specified in the bill, namely, $7,000,000, seemed excessive to the committee. The statement made by the minister as to the province of Ontario being behind this legislation and accepting full responsibility for it of course will be determined entirely by the letter which we shall read; the construction placed upon it as to terms; who signs it, and his power and authority to bind the province in the premises. It is a little difficult to understand why the original bill was prepared in the terms in which it was and why people of so little worth as the promoters should be those who are behind this legislation. Just one thing further.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) for concurrence in the second report of the special committee appointed to investigate farm implement prices, presented to the house on the 8th of April, 1937.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had just concluded a brief examination of the financial position of the farm implement companies. I had pointed out that

Farm Implements Committee Report
the losses suffered by the Massey-Harris Company were due in a measure to their high distribution costs. The committee found that the distribution costs in connection with farm implements were altogether excessive and that the Massey-Harris costs were the highest of all. I do not intend to go into this matter extensively as I should like to conclude my remarks in the allotted time.
It was found that the distribution cost of the International Harvester Company for the ten year period under examination was 22.13 per cent of the net sales. The distribution cost of Deere and Company was 22.57 per cent of the net sales. We were not successful in obtaining the costs of the Cockshutt Plow Company. The distribution cost of the Frost and Wood Company was 20.36 per cent, while the cost of the Massey-Harris Company was 33.46 per cent, more than ten per cent above the average of the other companies. The committee came to the conclusion that while the Massey-Harris Company suffered in Canada a loss of 15.800,000, if they had distributed their products as economically as the other companies, they would have made a saving about equal to their loss.
I do not wish the house to think I am making an attack upon the Massey-Harris Company, as that is absolutely foreign to my purpose. I suggested in my opening remarks that they were a great Canadian concern of which we were proud. If I may be allowed to refer to my own family, in the sixty years that my father and I have been farming we have paid the Massey-Harris people thousands of dollars. We have always thought that no other machine company in the world could make better machines than the Massey-Harris Company. The committee arrived at the conclusion that the cost of distribution was altogether too high and makes a recommendation that the government take into serious consideration the possibility of assisting cooperative organizations in the handling and servicing of farm implements.
I should like to say something about freight rates on agricultural implements. This matter was mentioned by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley). This is of supreme importance to the western provinces as two-thirds of the machinery sold is sold in the west. Nine per cent of the farmer's dollar is absorbed in freight rates. In 1913 the freight charges on a binder to Regina was $17.80, whereas in 1935 this cost had risen to $25.87. The freight charges on machinery going west to-day are forty per cent higher than they were under the Crowsnest pass agreement.
Yesterday I stated that this Crowsnest pass agreement was an agreement made with the Canadian Pacific railway, and that it had been amended so that we lost the benefit of the Crowsnest pass rates on machinery and other products going westward. In the speech he made over six weeks ago the hon. member for Qu'Appelle stated he was in favour of the restoration of the Crowsnest pass rates on machinery. I do not see the hon. member in his seat to-night, but his statement appears on Hansard. It is just too bad that we did not have similar Conservatives in the house in 1922 when the Crowsnest pass arrangement was lost. I well remember the bitter and determined fight the Conservative party, led by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, put up at that time. Had it not been for the Liberal party, the Crowsnest pass agreement would have been abrogated entirely. I want to compliment the hon. member for Qu'Appelle upon coming out and stating that he is in favour of the restoration of the Crowsnest pass rates on products going westward. I wonder how many of the Conservatives whom I see sitting in front of me at the present time would take the same stand.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has misstated the facts, I am sure unconsciously. He stated that the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen was against the Crowsnest pass agreement. The fact is that he said the rates should be settled by the railway commission. That was his position. The legislation was allowed to pass in this house, but it was altered in the senate. It was brought up by one of the members of the senate in the form in which it was subsequently dealt with.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: When the matter passed this house, the Crowsnest pass rates were completely abrogated, and it was only by accident that our own senator from Portage la Prairie discovered that fact. He asked that they be not abrogated entirely, but be suspended for a period of three years. That suggestion was agreed to in the senate, and it was brought in as an amendment to the bill, to which the house agreed. Had it not been for the action taken in the senate, I think the right hon. leader of the opposition will agree with me when I say that the Crowsnest pass rates would have been abrogated.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: No, not abrogated.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
Reference is made to the ugly word " repudiation " when we ask for a refunding of our public debt. I dislike to think it is repudiation in this connection. An arrangement was made by the people of
2416	COMMONS
Farm Implements Committee Report
Canada, and I cannot see why a different arrangement cannot be made when the boot is on the other foot.
I should like to touch briefly upon the cost of repairs. The committee examined this and found it was a great factor in the high replacement cost of machinery, especially in those tough years when we were not able to buy a complete machine and found it necessary to buy repair parts and patch up the old machine. Repairs, as everybody knows, are sold for cash, and there is no loss or bad debts. The mark-up in the price of repairs, in comparison with the complete machine, is 66 per cent. I have further information in regard to that, but I must hurry on as there are other matters perhaps more important.
Now, as to the effects of the tariff on the cost of machinery, we went into that thoroughly, and I want to say right here that I believe the dumping act is the most diabolical weapon ever devised by man for the strangulation of international trade. The present government, I believe, are not using the dumping act to a very great extent. They have practically relieved the people of Canada from the use of that deplorable weapon. But in the ten year period under examination, under both governments, the dumping act was responsible for the implement companies of the United States retaining in that country S17,-000,000 by the International Harvester Company and $9,000,000 by Deere and Company. By that action the treasury of Canada lost $400,000 which they would have been able to tax these companies on their profits had the profits been retained in Canada where they were earned. It may be said that this has nothing to do with increasing the price of farm machinery, but I doubt if that is so. I maintain that it has had something to do with it. I am going to read an extract carried by the Canadian Press over two years ago when we were discussing this question in the house:
Ottawa, June 12-Due to what Hughes Cleaver (Liberal, Halton), called the "silly tariff policy" which permitted the revenue minister to fix values for duty purposes, the International Harvester Company was obliged to charge Canadian importers $200 more on a $1,000 tractor than the price to United States farmers, Charles R. Morrison, vice president of the company, told the house committee on agriculture Thursday.
It goes on to say:
The company was accustomed to give a discount of 25 per cent to its United States selling organization and had always been willing to give the same discount to the Canadian company. However, in attempting to apply it,

the implement manufacturers ran up against the Canadian customs regulations which empowered the national revenue minister to fix the fair market value of importations.
Here is an extract from the committee's report:
The policy of the Department of National Revenue has indirectly introduced a factor unfavourable to the maintenance of low prices in Canada in the ease of these two companies, one of which sells one-third of the total requirements of the Canadian farmer while the other occupies a strong position in the western Canadian market.
The committee, therefore, feels that this whole matter has an important bearing on the question of retail prices on farm implements in Canada.
And a recommendation from the committee was:
That indirectly this retention of profits in the United States affected the price level of farm implements in Canada as the true profits arising out of their Canadian operations were not properly appreciated by the United States companies.
As regards the effects of the tariff, does a reduction in the tariff mean a reduction in the cost of imported products? It did not mean that in the case of farm machinery. I remember how my Conservative friends seemed jubilant at the fact that after we had lowered the tariff on farm machinery the price went up. I remember clipping out at the time an item in the Winnipeg Tribune, a supporter of the Conservative cause, which, speaking of the reduction in the tariff and the increase in the price of machinery, says:
Along came Mr. King and lowered the tarff protection by approximately one-half.
This was before they lowered the tariff five per cent, bringing it down to 74 per cent.
The western Liberal members of parliament sat back expectantly waiting for prices to fall, instead the new catalogue shows higher prices. The western Liberals have been howling to high Heaven ever since.
They seem to think there is some magic about the words " lower tariff." There is not.
We maintain that there is a great difference between the two old political parties on the tariff. The Conservatives stand for high protection, and the Liberals for low tariff; if there is no difference between a low tariff and a high tariff we should know it, and the way to find out is to strip these companies, who have defied parliament, of all tariff protection, and let them stand on their own feet.
Some will say that a combine exists. Well, if a combine does exist, we have the machinery to take care of the situation. I remember sitting in this house and listening to the Minister

Farm Implements Committee Report
of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) in the opening session in 1936. I forget what he was discussing at the time, -but this is what he said in reference to -the Combines Investigation Act. It will be found at page 510 of Hansard of that year:
But I emphasize again that there are occasions-and they exist to-day, I believe- when it becomes the duty of government to intervene if a great business organization takes advantage of its power to oppress its workers pr exploit the consumer.
I claim that is exactly what the machinery companies have done, and not only have they exploited the consumer but they have defied parliament.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
If I may be allowed, I am not critical just for the sake of being critical, and I am not condemning the government which I support because I like condemning them; I am condemning them, if I must, because I am a friend of the government and I would like to see them follow the paths we think they should follow.
I am going to give the house the record of this government in regard to the duty on farm implements. The Liberal party have been pledged to the abolition of the duty on farm implements since 1919, when they drafted their platform. We are told in this house that we should take a long range vision when we are legislating and to- see what is ahead of us. Surely, Mr. Speaker, twenty years is a long enough vision in regard to removing the duty on agricultural implements. The Hon. Charles Stewart, Liberal member of this house in 1935, in opposition at that time, but who, if he had been reelected, would have no doubt been sitting on the treasury benches to-day, moved a resolution- in 1935 as follows: Hon. Charles Stewart (West Edmonton) moved:
That in the opinion of this bouse the best interests of Canada demand that the burden of customs taxation be lessened on the instruments of production in the agricultural industry and to this end, farm implements and machinery should be free from custom duties.
He said:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to detain the house at any length on the introduction of this motion. I think, however, it would be of interest to recite briefly the history of customs duties as applied to farm machinery, and to point out their detrimental effect upon the farming industry of this country. I do not think there will be any disagreement with the statement that agriculture is the most important occupation of the Canadian people.
I quoted this resolution, during the campaign, and was proud to do so. This government has a
splendid chance to practice reciprocity with the United States. We kno-w that for years Canadian farm machinery was allowed to enter the United States duty free, and it would be only an act of justice to the farmers of this country, without hurting anyone, if we allowed United States farm machinery to enter Canada duty free.
I want to	say thit to the Prime
Minister. At Easter time when I was home I found, along with the information I received while I was here, that a bitter feeling-prevails in western Canada in regard to the government's action respecting farm machinery. I have two letters here signed by the secretary of the United Farmers of Manitoba, from which I should like to make two short extracts. He encloses a copy of a letter directed to the chairman of the special committee. He says: We are very much concerned about this situation. The implement people appear determined to over-ride the conclusions and recommendations of last year's committee and to press still more extortionate prices in 1938.
We think this is a challenge to Canadian democracy and we are looking for unified action on the part of representatives of rural Canada. We respectfully urge that our plea in this letter be given your personal attention.
And he writes this significant postcript: Surely the western rural members acting together should be able to get action.
That letter was written on- March 16. I have another letter dated April 21, which is a copy of a letter that was directed -to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner); he has this information. The writer says:
The executive of the United Farmers of Manitoba meeting on April 11th and 12th, were deeply concerned in regard to the present situation re prices of farm implements.
The report of the special committee of last year, they feel, is a call to action which ought not to be ignored, and there seems to be no action in sight just now. They view this with extreme disappointment. That a widespread injustice should not only be permitted to continue but actually be allowed to increase creates a very grave situation.
I see that I have exhausted my time. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the house for having given me this extra time, and I shall conclude with very few remarks:
I want to say that the machine companies have forfeited any right to tariff protection which they may have had. They have not played fair with the farmers and working men of this country. They have combined on a squeeze play to boost prices at a time when higher prices were not warranted. Their action has hindered the progress of agriculture, and in my opinion it is high time that this
2418	COMMONS
Farm Implements Committee Report
parliament should institute measures which will compel a reduction in the prices now being charged for agricultural machinery. What I have said is not inspired by malice towards the manufacturers of farm machinery or any other individual or group; its object is rather to present the viewpoint of the farmers who must and do purchase this machinery. We as a class have not been blessed with legislative protection-notwithstanding some remarks that have been made- nor do we need or desire any special privileges; but we do object, and our voice is becoming increasingly articulate in demanding that others get off our backs so that we may live and provide for our families. Furthermore, we wish to pay our fair share of tribute to the state, but insist, when so doing, that we be allowed a fair recompense for our labours.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
It is
not my intention to present either an analysis or a synopsis of the evidence and report of the committee. That has already been done ably and succinctly by most of the previous speakers. I wish to give a short historical resume of this entire inquiry into the causes underlying the high prices of farm implements.
First, on March 2, 1936, an order was issued in this house for an inquiry into the high price of farm implements Second, on April 24, 1936. a question was asked, as reported on page 2127 of Hansard, regarding the response of the implement companies to the agricultural committee's request that during the course of the inquiry the prices should be reduced to their former level. May I quote that from Hansard? On the orders of the day I asked the following question:
I would ask the government if it has drawn to the attention of the agricultural implement industry the motion passed by this house asking that industry to keep the price of farm implements at their former level until the present investigation has been completed; what assurance has been received from the agricultural implement industry, and why has this request not been complied with?
The Minister of Agriculture replied:
Mr. Gardiner:	Mr. Speaker, letters were
sent to the implement companies calling their attention to the resolution passed by the committee. So far as I know there has not been, down to the present, information received in reply from all the companies. I think a letter was received from one company, but I would prefer when the information is produced to have it brought down as a whole.
Mr. M. J. Coldwell:	Does the government
contemplate bringing down any legislation or taking other action to bring the implement companies to a reasonable frame of mind regarding these prices?
There was no answer.

On February 1, 1937, the agricultural committee reported and suggested the setting up of a select committee of this house to continue the investigation into the high price of farm implements. On April 8, 1937, the report was tabled in the house by the chairman of that committee, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston), but no discussion followed and no action was taken. Of course the government was anxious to expedite the business of the house in order that the parliamentary committee might attend the coronation. On March 11, 1938, the report was discussed on a motion of concurrence moved by the chairman of the committee. The time between the tabling of the report and the moving of the motion of concurrence was so long that the chairman felt that something ought to be done about it, and so he added seven suggestions of his own. It should be remembered that these suggestions are not a part of the report and have no bearing upon the report. The strangest thing of all is that one of these suggestions was the institution of a system of crop insurance, a matter over which this committee had no jurisdiction, and which was very largely a sop to soothe the disappointment of those who had expected the government to take some action as a result of this inquiry.
The motion for concurrence was moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre on March 11 of this year. Now, six weeks later, on April 29 we are still discussing a report that was tabled over a year ago regarding the investigation into the high price of farm implements. One cannot too strongly condemn the dilatoriness of the entire procedure with regard to this inquiry. It looks to me like a grand farce, with the government stalling for time. May I point out first of all that it is two years since this investigation began, and now, after two years, we are only at the stage of discussing a report which, even if it is passed, is no guarantee of legislative action regarding the committee's recommendations, let alone the chairman's suggestions. Let me point out further that so much time has been allowed to elapse during the present session that it is altogether unlikely that we shall get legislative action during this sitting of parliament. This means that it is not likely we shall have legislation dealing with this matter until next year, which will probably be the session prior to the general election. In other words, the entire term of office during which the present government has ruled will have been taken up with an inquiry into a question regarding which the government's duty was clear from the was beginning. I believe it was Disraeli who

Farm Implements Committee Report
said that commissions were set up to find out things which everybody else knew already. Certainly this committee has succeeded so far only in presenting excellent material, but not in getting the government to implement any, of the recommendations that were made.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: The committee did more than that.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: During this entire period of two years the farmers have continued to suffer the injustice of high farm implement prices, which have placed an additional burden of $4,000,000 per annum upon the backs of the prairie farmers.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: How does the hon. member figure that out?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: I shall give the basis for that in just a few moments.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: The hon. member is a great figurer.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: An examination of the facts will show that the implement companies have totally disregarded the wishes of the committee and of parliament. First of all, the companies did not accede to the request of the committee that the prices should be reduced to their former level until the investigation had been completed. I have here a copy of the correspondence passing between counsel for the committee and the different implement companies, and in very polite language the committee was told by the companies that it ought to mind its own business. Again, these companies during the investigation absolutely failed to substantiate their claim that the increase in the cost of implements was due to an increase in the cost of raw materials and labour.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: That is your opinion.

speechtext:
It is not my opinion. Let me quote from the evidence at page 386. Mr. Morrison, the head of the International Harvester Company is on the stand and Mr. Graham is legal counsel for the parliamentary committee. I quote from the evidence.
Q. So that these pig iron prices are going down in that period?
A. Yes, all right.
Q. Now we will take scrap-in 1930 it was 17-60; in 1931 it was 19-31; in 1932 it was 12-36; in 1933 it was 10-22 and in 1934 there was a slight increase to 11-23; but again in scrap there is the same reduction in the period isn't there? In steel, steel in 1930 was 2-37; in 1931 it was 2-37; in 1932 it was 2-44; in 1933 it was 2-31 and in 1934 it was 2-33; if anything there has been a slight drop-isn't that correct?
A. Yes.
Q. You will recall that lumber, which comprised about 10 per cent of the raw material costs, in 1930 was 99-98; in 1931 it was 102-87; in 1932 it dropped to 88-82; in 1933 it dropped to 82-20; and in 1934 it dropped to 73-82-so that there was a decided drop in the cost of lumber to you. Isn't that correct?
A. According to these figures.
Q. Well, these figures are supplied by yourself, Mr. Morrison. These are the big items; pig iron, scrap, steel and lumber; so that you will agree with me that in the prices you had to pay for raw materials entering into your product in the period from 1923 to 1935 there was a decided drop rather than an increase, except in steel, which seems to have held just steady; would not that be correct?
A. That would be correct.
Q. So that I submit again, Mr. Morrison, in the light of that, that when you suggest to your answers to me last spring that increase in the cost of materials was an element that jusified the raise, surely you cannot uphold that now in the face of this information-dealing with materials alone, I will go into the others with you later-but dealing with material costs alone?
A. All right, let us concede the material.
Q. You will concede the material?
A. Yes.
On page 387 the question of labour is discussed :
Q. Well, then, I do not know that I need go- much further on that particular point, if you agree with that. It refutes the suggestion that you made in your statement that increased labour costs justified the increase in price?
A. Well, I think Mr. Graham you are being just a little liberal; I said, material, labour and burden; what I meant was collective material, labour and burden.
Q. Of course, it is my duty, Mr. Morrison, to separate them, naturally. You would agree with me then that labour costs during the period have decreased rather than increased; and that therefore labour treated as a single element does not justify the increase?
A. That is true.
Q. That is true?
A. Yes.
I say, therefore, that the evidence shows that the increase in costs of material and labour did not justify the increase in 1936. The committee showed further that they had no doubt in their minds that an injustice had been perpetrated upon the purchasers of farm implements. I do not wish to quote extensively. Let me quote two statements from the recommendations at page 1216:
The companies, having during the depression years maintained, relatively, their price levels, the committee suggests that now they are approaching a period of normal or above normal volume of production and sales, the companies can well afford, comparatively and actually, to lower their prices and still make satisfactory financial returns, because of the great saving
2420	COMMONS
Farm Implements Committee Report
in overhead per unit of production. This policy would be of particular benefit in the period in which the farmer is making necessary replacements.

The results have been very confusing to those studying price trends over this period. During the period 1913 to 1936 the price of tractors declined by about fifty per cent. On the other hand prices of the general line of horse drawn implements and machines showed a level in 1936 between fifty and sixty per cent higher than in 1913.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: Does the hon. member realize he is comparing incomparables? It is as if he were comparing the price of bicycles with that of motorcycles.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: I am not aware that either motorcycles or bicycles are farm implements. The hon. gentleman has had a long experience in such matters, and he may be able to get the committee to regard bicycles and motorcycles as farm implements.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows quite well what I mean. He is dodging my question.

speechtext:
The committee went on to point out at page 1217, that in Canada only one farmer out of every seven possesses a tractor. Then, on pages 1294 to 1296 are set out thirty-six recommendations. I shall not take the time of the house to read them; most hon. members have already gone through this. But five things that the committee proved to their own satisfaction at least are worth noting. In the first place they prove that farm implement prices from 1891 to 1936 had consistently been too high. I suggest a reading of recommendation No. 30:
That over the period 1891 to 1936 retail prices of farm implements have been maintained at too high a level as shown by the financial returns to the companies engaged in the industry during that period.
Second, they maintained that the increase in 1936 was unjustifiable. I refer to recommendation No. 29:
That the increases announced by the companies in January, 1936, were not justified by an increase in manufacturing or distribution costs or by the financial results of the companies in so far as these were affected by the price level of farm implements.
Third, the committee was convinced that the cost of distribution was too high. I refer to recommendation No. 33:
That the committee is of the opinion that the cost of distribution of farm implements is unnecessarily high and constitutes an important factor in the prices to the consumers.

They pointed out also that the cost of machinery bought on time was so excessive as to constitute usury. I refer to recommendation No. 27:
That the cost of credit to the farmer purchasing farm implements on time is excessive and the companies should take immediate steps to reduce these credit charges.
The fifth thing I want to draw to the attention of the house is that this committee was of the opinion that unless the companies themselves took some action, the government would be justified in encouraging the cooperative distribution and servicing of farm machinery. I refer to recommendation No. 34:
That the companies themselves should make every effort to reduce these costs or farmers should be encouraged to organize for the cooperative distribution and servicing of farm implements.
This is an investigation which began two years ago. During the investigation the companies refused to lower their prices to the former level. One year ago a report was tabled proving conclusively to the satisfaction of the committee five things:
1.	That the prices had been too high.
2.	That the increase was unjustifiable.
3.	That the cost of distribution was too high.
4.	That carrying charges were too high.
5.	That if the companies themselves did not do something, a cooperative organization should be set up.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: That was not unanimous.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
It is the report of the committee and I am reading it as such. The members of the committee have the right to point out to what extent they disagreed with the report. But it was a majority report.
After these conclusions had been reached and the report tabled in this house, instead of the farm implement companies then acceding to the request to lower prices to the former level they brought about a second increase on November 1, 1937, an increase of 7-8 per cent, which in addition to the three per cent increase in January, 1936, made an increase to the primary producers of almost eleven per cent. It is apparent that the farm implement companies have no intention of cooperating with the committee; that they have defied the request of the committee to the extent not only of refusing to accede to their request, but of actually bringing about a second increase in prices. That is why, when this session opened, I placed on the order paper a resolution which reads:
Whereas the price of farm implements is too high in relation to the price of farm products.
And whereas the cost of distribution of farm implements is too high and is a major factor in the cost of farm implements;

Farm Implements Committee Report
And whereas the credit charges to farmers buying machinery on time is excessive,
Therefore be it resolved,-That this house recommend to the government that they encourage farmers to organize in provincial units for the cooperative distribution and servicing of farm implements.
I had hoped that during this session we should reach that resolution, in order that parliament might have an opportunity of taking some action, since it is quite apparent that the implement companies do not intend to take any.
When he was moving his motion of concurrence, the hon. member for Lake Centre read a letter from the United Farmers of Manitoba which was somewhat commendatory. But I have here a letter written by the same organization since this motion for concurrence was presented. I agree with the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) that these farmers are becoming suspicious and impatient. This letter, which is dated March 16, 1938, is addressed to the chairman of the committee; it is a circular letter. I shall not take time to read all of it, but I should like to read two or three paragraphs:
I am sure there are few who realize as your address shows that the implement companies' reply to the committee report of last session was an increase of 7-8 per cent on top of the 3 per cent increase of 1936, and that it means a fresh and utterly unjustifiable levy of !>4,000,000 on the farmers of the prairie for the benefit of the makers of the tools they use.
We note the seven suggestions made in your address-but feel that coming simply as suggestions and not being included in your motion they are not likely to be fully effective. I must add that apart from some definite pressure upon the implement people with a view to securing equitable rates, the suggestion of a commission such as you have in mind in No. 7 is not likely to be regarded as enough. Our people are increasingly suspicious of commissions involving fabulous fees and expenses and their reports being filed away without any action resulting. There ought to be immediate action by the government before any such commission is thought of. . . .
There must be more than concurrence in the report of last session and more than a commission to report a year or two from now. I can very definitely assure you that the farmers of the prairies will not be satisfied with these.
That is signed by Wm. R. Wood, secretary, United Farmers of Manitoba.
I therefore say that at this time concurrence in a report which is now a year old is idle and futile. Since the tabling of that report the situation has completely changed. Another increase in prices has taken place. In my opinion, which I think is shared by many people who are buying these implements on the prairies, we cannot escape our responsibilities 51953-154
by pious wishes and wishful suggestions; this parliament must be prepared to do something, and something of a constructive and helpful nature. I therefore move an amendment seconded by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell):
That the second report of the special committee of the house to inquire into the causes underlying the high prices of farm implements be not now concurred in but be referred back to the committee with instructions that they may add the following:
Whereas the agricultural implement companies have disregarded the recommendations of the committee and have failed to reduce their prices since this report was presented to the house on April 8, 1937, but on the contrary have announced an increase in prices which took effect on November 1, 1937, that the government carry out the recommendation of the report by taking immediate steps to assist farmers in the organization of cooperatives for the distribution and servicing of farm implements.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
I have listened with a great
deal of interest to the address just delivered by the hon, member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas) and also to the suggested amendment. I doubt very much, however, whether it is in order; I suggest that it is not. It deals with a matter of policy, instructing a committee to dictate government policy, something which I doubt that this house would care to do or has power to do. While you are considering the question of whether or not it is in order, Mr. Speaker, if I have your permission I shall proceed with the discussion of the original question.
The hon, member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas) has relieved me of the necessity of reading paragraphs 29, 30, 32 and 33 of the report of the committee, all of which bear directly upon the findings as this house has been called upon to consider them. It has been stated that two years ago some discussion arose in the house as a result of the increase in the prices of farm implements. That discussion arose largely because of opposition which came from the western part of Canada. I know the house does not consider the fact that the question was raised by hon. members from the west means that the objection to the increased prices of farm implements is purely a western one. The only reason the first objections came from the west, as compared with any other part of Canada, is that the west, more than any other part of Canada, depends upon machinery for successfully carrying on the industry of agriculture. However, that is not so true to-day as it was ten or twenty years ago.

2422	COMMONS
Farm Implements Committee Report
Farms in eastern Canada are becoming more mechanized than they were a few years ago, and as a result of the evidence presented to the committee and the discussions which have taken place in the committee, I think it is fair to say that the objections to the two increases in the price of farm implements since this government came into power have come just as strongly from the eastern part of Canada as from the west. For that reason I would say that a discussion of this question to-day is not a sectional matter in any sense of the term, and anything I have to say is spoken on behalf of farmers whether they live in eastern or western Canada.
At page 1229 of the proceedings of the committee there is something which bears upon the method I intend to follow in dealing with the report:
That these implements are truly representative of the industry is evident from the fact that in the case of the International Harvester Company information supplied thereon covered seventy-five per cent of its implement production at Hamilton, exclusive of parts .	.	.
That is, after having reported the list of implements to which special consideration was given.
As in other branches of the inquiry the information submitted by the International Harvester Company of Canada was particularly valuable in that its cost accounting policy and system has been consistently followed since 1913 and in that its costs are all-inclusive. This company has. in the final analysis, only two kinds of expense, i.e.. manufacturing and distribution, and every expenditure of the company eventually finds its way into one or the other of these categories.
In other words, in the evidence submitted by that company all costs in connection with farm implements were in one or the other of two classes, factory costs or distribution costs. The report continues:
The companies agreed that all information submitted with regard to a binder could be placed on the printed records of the committee in order to give concrete information as to manufacturing costs and selling values in the industry. The binder was found by the auditor to be in most particulars close to the average of all the smaller typical implements selected by the committee. For this reason the undernoted tables as to the binder can be treated as truly informative.
Following that statement are three tables, one having to do with the eight foot binder of the International Harvester Company, the second having to do with the Massey-Harris binder and the third having to do with the Frost and Wood binder, and these statements are said to be typical of the costs, both distribution and factory, of all small farm imple-

ments sold in Canada. The report goes further and indicates that these delivered costs are at one particular point in Canada, and again that is a point which illustrates very well the costs to the farmers of western Canada. That point is the city of Regina, in the centre of the farming area that requires and uses more farm implements than any other agricultural area in Canada.
I am going to content myself by dealing with the International Harvester Company binder, rather than attempting to deal with all three companies, in view of the fact that it is typical of other farm implements, and it will be noted that the price of this binder to the farmer at Regina in 1913 was 1167.02; in 1936 it was 1281, an increase of $113.98 over the period under review. It has been said by some hon. members that labour had a great deal to do with that increase, and that where labour is concerned we should not criticize; that in this house we should attempt to do those things which will make it more profitable for men to be engaged in industry. I am prepared to defend labour's claim to consideration as strongly as any hon. member of the house, but I would direct attention to the fact that the cost of labour entering into the construction of an International Harvester binder in 1913 was valued at SI 1.97. In 1936 it was $22.62. The difference in the cost of labour as between 1913 and 1936 was only $10.65, but the increase in the price of the binder was $113.98. So we can make all allowance for the increased cost of labour and still discuss the question of -whether or not the price of the binder is too high. Then let us look at the cost of material.

Some hon. members have maintained that there has been an increase in the cost of material. There has been. In 1913 the material cost $45.56; in 1936 it cost $71.06, or an increase of S25.50 over that period of time. Some members have maintained that there has been an increase in freight costs. There has been. In 1913 freight costs were S17.S0; in 1936 they were $26.08, or an increase of $8.28 in that time. So we have labour costs increasing by $10.65; material costs increasing by $25.50, and freight costs increasing by $8.28, or a total of $44.43. So I repeat that after having given consideration to these three items, we find that the price of the binder was increased by $113.98, not by only $44.43. In other words, the price of a binder could be reduced by $69.55, to sell at $211.45, without affecting increases in labour, material or freight costs, still leaving the same mark-up as in 1913. These are factors over which the companies have little if any control. They have probably no great control over the cost of labour; they have probably no great control over the cost of materials, and they have very little if any control over the cost of freight.
But there are two other items that enter into the cost of placing a binder at the disposal of the farmer. The first is the overhead or burden, the difference between the two years being $18.18. The second item is the sales cost, and in this instance the difference is $15.05. These two increases amount to $33.23. Even if the companies have no power to adjust these matters, the total increase in cost is $77.66, whereas the increase in price is $113.98. Therefore, a binder could have been reduced in 1936 by $3632 without the companies having to adjust any of the items of cost submitted in the table which appears on page 1230. If that were done, they would still have as a mark-up exactly the same amount as they had in 1913, when they sold a binder in Regina for $167.02. If overhead costs were maintained at the 1913 level, a binder could be sold for $52 less without reducing any of the other costs and still leave the mark-up of 1913.
Someone may ask, Why compare 1913 with 1936? Nineteen thirty-six is not the year of highest cost of materials entering into the factory costs of farm implements. According to this table, the cost of delivering a binder to a farmer in Regina in 1921 was $262.53. This was the year in which binders sold at the highest price in the history of our country. The cost of delivering the same binder in 1936 was 201.74. A binder sold for $326 in 1921 and for $281 in 1936. The mark-up in 1921
is $63.47, and in 1936, $79.26. Labour received $9 more from the binder in 1921 than in 1936, whereas materials cost $41.06 more than in 1936. In other words, on the basis of 1921 a binder could have been sold for $16 less than it was sold for in 1936, and the companies would have been left with the same mark-up as they had in the year of the highest cost.
Let us take the year 1922 and compare it with 1936. According to this table the cost of delivering a binder to a farmer in Regina in 1922 was $204.91, which is $3 more than it cost in 1936. The binder was sold for $15 more in 1936.

In other words, there was an increase in the 1936 price as compared with other years and an increase in mark-up over and above the actual costs in other years, running all the way from $12 in the lowest year to $42.43 in 1932. I contend that a binder could have been sold at a lower price, and my contention is backed up by an examination of the cost basis in' any one of the years with which I have dealt.
The binder is the average implement among all the implements used by the farmers in the Dominion of Canada. Therefore, I think we are safe in saying that all other small implements could have been reduced an equal amount without putting the companies in any worse position than they were in during any of the preceding years. There is another way in which this matter may be looked at. The table shows that the cost of placing an eight foot International Harvester Company binder in the hands of a farmer in Regina in 1936 was $201.74. This binder was sold for $281 cash, which is close to a 40 per cent write-up on the total cost, which includes factory costs, distribution costs and sales costs. I tiiink it

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
I submit to my hon friend Mr. Douglas (Weyburn) and the house that his amendment is not in order, because it suggests referring back the report of the committee to the committee. The committee has ceased to exist, and therefore it is impossible to refer the report back to it. The committee has ceased to exist for the simple reason that the rules provide that where a committee has submitted its final report, its proceedings are assumed to have ended, and unless the committee is revived it ceases to exist. I refer Your Honour to standing order 66 on reports from committees, citation 664:
If a committee at the conclusion of their inquiry make a final report to the house, the sittings of the committee are assumed to have been closed, and if further proceedings were desired it would be necessary to revive the committee.
Also prorogation has the effect of ending the work of all committees and dissolving them. If a committee is to continue its work at a subsequent session, it must be revived by special motion to that effect. On that I refer to Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, page 103:
In like manner a prorogation has the effect of dissolving all committees, whether standing or special.
In the circumstances I submit that the amendment is out of order.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: Might I ask the Prime Minister why we should be considering the report of the committee if the committee has been dissolved?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: What we are doing now is considering the matter of concurrence in the report of a committee. The committee had submitted its final report, and in so doing it is assumed to have ended its proceedings. As I said, prorogation itself would have ended the committee. If it were the desire of the house to revive the committee, that could be done by a motion, and then any matter could be referred back to the committee, or the report itself referred back. But at the present time the committee is non-existent.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext: I think the point of order taken by the Prime Minister is correct, that there is no body now existing to which we could refer the subject matter of the amendment of the hon. member for Weyburn. I therefore declare the amendment out of order.
